H3 would write the same style for 1484 more entries; this page exists to sanity-check the style and content before that runs. Poster image, purpose text, the full step-by-step instructions, and any contraindication tags shown per exercise.

Abs Snails

Abdominals

PurposeRolling the hips up over the shoulders trains the lower part of the stomach through a much longer range than a crunch. It also teaches the spine to move one segment at a time instead of hinging in one place.

  1. Lie on your back with your arms flat on the floor beside you, palms down
  2. Lift your legs until your feet point at the ceiling
  3. Press your lower back into the floor and squeeze your stomach
  4. Curl your hips off the floor and roll your legs back over your chest
  5. Lower slowly, one part of the spine at a time, until your hips touch down again
ea_abs_snails

Barbell Landmine Side Bend

Abdominals

PurposeLoads the muscles down the side of the trunk, which hold you upright when weight is on one side only. Strength there is what stops you tipping when you carry a heavy bag or a child on one hip.

  1. Stand side-on to the landmine and hold the loaded bar end in the outside hand
  2. Stand tall with your feet hip width apart and your free hand on your head
  3. Keep both shoulders facing forward, not rotating
  4. Bend sideways toward the weight, letting it travel down your leg
  5. Pull yourself back upright using the opposite side, then swap sides
ea_barbell_landmine_side_bend

Barbell Situp

Abdominals

PurposeAdding a barbell turns the sit-up into a loaded exercise the stomach can actually be made stronger by, rather than a repetition-counting drill. Start far lighter than you expect.

  1. Lie on your back with knees bent and feet anchored under something solid
  2. Hold a light barbell across your upper chest or pressed overhead with straight arms
  3. Brace your stomach and tuck your chin slightly
  4. Curl up until your torso is upright, keeping the bar in the same position relative to your body
  5. Lower slowly all the way back down under control
ea_barbell_situp

Cable Standing Crunch

Abdominals

PurposeA crunch you can add weight to a kilo at a time, which is what the stomach needs to get stronger — bodyweight crunches stop working once you can do fifty. Standing also keeps the neck out of it.

  1. Attach a rope to a high pulley and kneel or stand facing away from the machine
  2. Hold both ends beside your head with your elbows pointing down
  3. Keep your hips still — they should not move at all
  4. Crunch your ribs down toward your hips by rounding the upper back
  5. Return slowly to upright, resisting the cable the whole way
ea_cable_standing_crunch lower_backneck

Copenhagen Plank

Abdominals

PurposeOne of the very few exercises that loads the inner thigh in a position it actually has to work in. It is used in football specifically because it lowers the rate of groin injuries.

  1. Lie on your side and place the upper leg on a bench, ankle or knee supported
  2. Prop yourself on the lower elbow, directly under your shoulder
  3. Lift your hips until your body forms a straight line from head to feet
  4. Squeeze the top leg down into the bench to hold yourself up
  5. Hold for the set time, then lower under control and change sides
ea_copenhagen_plank elbowwrist

Dragonfly

Abdominals

PurposeAn advanced hold where the whole body lowers as one rigid line, which demands more from the stomach than any crunch can. Only worth attempting once hanging leg raises are easy and controlled.

  1. Lie back on a bench and grip it firmly behind your head with both hands
  2. Lift your legs and hips until your body is vertical, resting on your upper back
  3. Squeeze your stomach and glutes so your body is one straight line
  4. Lower that whole line slowly toward horizontal without bending at the hips
  5. Stop before your back arches, then pull back up to vertical
ea_dragonfly upper_back

Dumbbell Elbow Side Plank

Abdominals

PurposeA side plank with weight added, which trains the side of the trunk to resist being bent sideways. That is the job those muscles do in real life, far more often than bending you sideways on purpose.

  1. Lie on your side and prop up on the lower elbow, directly beneath your shoulder
  2. Stack your feet and lift your hips until your body is a straight line
  3. Hold a dumbbell on the top hip, or press it toward the ceiling with the free hand
  4. Keep your hips high and square, not rolling forward or back
  5. Hold for the set time, then lower and switch sides
ea_dumbbell_elbow_side_plank elbowwrist

Dumbbell Half Kneeling Wood Chopper

Abdominals

PurposeTrains rotation from a position where the hips cannot help, so the turn has to come from the trunk. Half kneeling also stretches the front of the down hip, which is short in most people who sit.

  1. Kneel on one knee with the other foot forward, both at ninety degrees
  2. Hold a dumbbell with both hands beside the hip of the down knee
  3. Brace your stomach and squeeze the glute of the kneeling leg
  4. Lift the weight diagonally across your body to above the opposite shoulder
  5. Lower it slowly along the same line, then finish the set and switch sides
ea_dumbbell_half_kneeling_wood_chopper knee

Dumbbell Hand Side Plank

Abdominals

PurposeThe straight-arm version adds a shoulder-stability demand on top of the side plank, so the shoulder has to hold a position while the trunk resists bending. Harder than the elbow version for most people.

  1. Lie on your side and press up onto the lower hand, arm straight under your shoulder
  2. Stack your feet and lift your hips into a straight line
  3. Hold a dumbbell on the top hip or reach it toward the ceiling
  4. Keep the supporting shoulder pushed away from your ear
  5. Hold for the set time, lower under control, then swap sides
ea_dumbbell_hand_side_plank elbowwrist

Dumbbell Kneeling Wood Chopper

Abdominals

PurposeKneeling on both knees takes the legs out entirely, so every bit of the rotation comes from the trunk. It builds the diagonal strength used in throwing, swinging and turning quickly.

  1. Kneel on both knees with your hips upright over them
  2. Hold a dumbbell with both hands beside one hip
  3. Brace your stomach and squeeze your glutes
  4. Sweep the weight diagonally up and across to above the opposite shoulder
  5. Return slowly along the same path, then repeat on the other side
ea_dumbbell_kneeling_wood_chopper knee

Dumbbell Overhead Side Bend

Abdominals

PurposeWith the arm overhead the side of the trunk is stretched before it contracts, which reaches further up the side than a normal side bend. Use a light weight — this is a long lever and it gets hard quickly.

  1. Stand tall and press one dumbbell overhead with a straight arm
  2. Place the free hand on your hip and set your feet hip width apart
  3. Keep both shoulders facing forward and your ribs down
  4. Bend sideways away from the raised arm, keeping it locked overhead
  5. Return to upright using the stretched side, then swap arms
ea_dumbbell_overhead_side_bend shoulder

Dumbbell Side Plank Up Down

Abdominals

PurposeMoving between elbow and hand in a side plank adds a shoulder-strength demand to a hold that is normally static. It also makes the trunk work harder, because the position keeps changing under it.

  1. Start in a side plank on your lower elbow with your hips lifted
  2. Hold a light dumbbell on the top hip or leave the top hand free
  3. Press up onto the lower hand by straightening that arm
  4. Lower back onto the elbow under control without letting the hips drop
  5. Continue for the set, then change sides
ea_dumbbell_side_plank_up_down elbowwrist

Dumbbell Suitcase Crunch

Abdominals

PurposeBringing the knees and chest together at once shortens the stomach from both ends, which loads it far more than lifting only the shoulders. Holding a dumbbell adds resistance to the top half.

  1. Sit on the floor or a bench, leaning back slightly with your feet off the ground
  2. Hold a dumbbell against your chest with both hands
  3. Brace your stomach and keep your back straight, not rounded
  4. Draw your knees toward your chest while curling your chest toward your knees
  5. Extend both away from each other slowly without letting your feet touch down
ea_dumbbell_suitcase_crunch lower_backneck

Flat Knee Raise

Abdominals

PurposeThe starting point for lower stomach work, and the first movement to master before hanging leg raises. It teaches the lower back to stay flat while the legs move, which is the whole point.

  1. Lie flat on your back with your legs straight and arms by your sides
  2. Press your lower back gently into the floor and keep it there
  3. Draw both knees up toward your chest, keeping the back flat
  4. Stop as soon as your lower back would start to lift off the floor
  5. Lower the feet slowly toward the ground without touching down
ea_flat_knee_raise

Hanging Leg Raises

Abdominals

PurposeThe standard exercise for the lower stomach, and one of the few that loads it through a long range. Hanging also stretches the shoulders and builds grip, so you get three things from one movement.

  1. Hang from a bar with an overhand grip, arms straight and shoulders active
  2. Squeeze your glutes so your body stops swinging
  3. Lift both legs together, curling your hips slightly up at the top
  4. Raise as high as you can control — knees bent is fine at first
  5. Lower slowly all the way down without letting momentum take over
ea_hanging_leg_raises

Hold the World Med Ball

Abdominals

PurposeHolding a ball out in front of you loads the stomach the way it actually works — resisting being pulled forward, rather than crunching. Simple, and much harder than it looks after thirty seconds.

  1. Stand tall holding a medicine ball with both hands at chest height
  2. Brace your stomach and pull your ribs down toward your hips
  3. Extend your arms to hold the ball out in front of you at shoulder height
  4. Do not let your lower back arch or your shoulders creep up
  5. Hold for the set time, then bring the ball back to your chest
ea_hold_the_world_med_ball

L Sit Hold

Abdominals

PurposeHolding the legs out straight while supporting your whole bodyweight on your hands is one of the hardest stomach exercises there is, and it builds shoulder strength at the same time. Start with bent knees.

  1. Sit between two parallettes and grip one in each hand
  2. Press down hard to lift your whole body off the floor, arms straight
  3. Push your shoulders down away from your ears
  4. Lift your legs until they are straight out in front, parallel to the floor
  5. Hold for as long as your form stays clean, then lower under control
ea_l_sit_hold

Landmine Hollow Hold

Abdominals

PurposeThe hollow hold is the position gymnasts use to teach the stomach to hold the ribs and hips together; adding a landmine gives it load, so it keeps working after the bodyweight version gets easy.

  1. Lie on your back and hold the loaded bar end above your chest with both hands
  2. Press your lower back flat into the floor
  3. Lift your shoulders and legs a few centimetres off the ground
  4. Keep the arms locked and your body in a shallow banana shape
  5. Hold for the set time, breathing shallowly, then lower everything together
ea_landmine_hollow_hold

Landmine Kneeling Twist

Abdominals

PurposeKneeling removes the legs, so the rotation is produced and controlled by the trunk alone. The landmine's arc means the resistance peaks at the sides, which is where the turn actually needs to be strong.

  1. Kneel on both knees facing the landmine, holding the bar end with both hands at chest height
  2. Straighten your arms so the bar is out in front of you
  3. Squeeze your glutes and keep your hips completely still
  4. Rotate the bar in an arc to one side, letting your ribs turn but not your hips
  5. Bring it back through the middle and rotate to the other side
ea_landmine_kneeling_twist knee

Landmine Oblique Twist

Abdominals

PurposeTrains the muscles that turn the trunk and, more importantly, the ones that stop it turning too far. Standing means the hips and legs participate, which is closer to how rotation happens in sport.

  1. Stand facing the landmine holding the bar end with both hands at chest height
  2. Extend your arms so the bar is in front of you, feet shoulder width apart
  3. Brace your stomach and let your feet pivot slightly as you turn
  4. Swing the bar in an arc down toward one hip, keeping the arms straight
  5. Control it back through the middle and repeat to the other side
ea_landmine_oblique_twist

Landmine Russian Twist

Abdominals

PurposeA rotation done at speed with a fixed arc, which trains the trunk to change direction quickly. Keep the movement controlled at the ends — the injuries in twisting exercises happen at the extremes, not in the middle.

  1. Stand facing the landmine with the bar end held at chest height in both hands
  2. Push your arms out and set your feet a little wider than your shoulders
  3. Rotate the bar down and across to one hip, pivoting the back foot
  4. Reverse smoothly and swing it across to the opposite hip
  5. Keep the arms straight and the movement controlled through both end positions
ea_landmine_russian_twist

Long Lever Plank

Abdominals

PurposeWalking the elbows further forward makes a plank dramatically harder without adding a second of time, because the lever gets longer. Twenty seconds of this beats two minutes of an ordinary plank.

  1. Start in a forearm plank with your elbows under your shoulders
  2. Walk your elbows forward, away from your body, a hand's length at a time
  3. Stop where you can still keep your hips level and your back flat
  4. Squeeze your glutes and stomach hard and keep breathing
  5. Hold for the set time, then walk the elbows back before lowering
ea_long_lever_plank elbowwrist

Med Ball Half Kneeling Wood Choppers

Abdominals

PurposeRotation trained from a half-kneeling position, where the hips are locked and the turn has to come from the trunk. The kneeling leg also gets a stretch through the front of the hip.

  1. Kneel on one knee with the other foot forward, both bent to ninety degrees
  2. Hold a medicine ball with both hands beside the hip of the kneeling leg
  3. Squeeze that glute and brace your stomach
  4. Sweep the ball diagonally across and up above the opposite shoulder
  5. Lower it slowly along the same path, then finish the set and switch
ea_med_ball_half_kneeling_wood_choppers knee

Med Ball Toe Touches

Abdominals

PurposeReaching a ball toward your toes with the legs vertical works the upper stomach through a short, hard range. Keeping the legs still is what makes it work — if they swing, the stomach stops doing much.

  1. Lie on your back and raise both legs so your feet point at the ceiling
  2. Hold a medicine ball with both hands, arms extended above your chest
  3. Press your lower back into the floor
  4. Curl your shoulders up and reach the ball toward your toes
  5. Lower slowly back to the floor, keeping your legs exactly where they were
ea_med_ball_toe_touches lower_back

Medicine Ball Chest Throw with Abs

Abdominals

PurposeThrowing trains the stomach and chest to produce force fast, which no slow repetition can teach. Power is a separate quality from strength, and it is the one that fades first with age.

  1. Sit or stand facing a wall or a partner, holding a medicine ball at your chest
  2. Brace your stomach and set your ribs down
  3. Push the ball explosively away from your chest with both hands
  4. Follow through fully, letting the trunk contract as you throw
  5. Catch or collect the ball, reset your position, and repeat
ea_medicine_ball_chest_throw_with_abs

Medicine Ball Rotational Throw

Abdominals

PurposeTrains rotation at full speed, which is how the trunk works in almost every sport — a golf swing, a punch, a throw. Slow twisting exercises build the strength; this teaches the body to use it quickly.

  1. Stand side-on to a solid wall, about a metre away, holding a medicine ball
  2. Set your feet shoulder width apart and bring the ball to the hip furthest from the wall
  3. Rotate hard toward the wall, pivoting the back foot as you turn
  4. Release the ball into the wall at chest height as your body faces it
  5. Catch the rebound, reset to the far hip, and repeat before changing sides
ea_medicine_ball_rotational_throw

Plate Hollow Hold

Abdominals

PurposeThe hollow position teaches the stomach to hold the ribs and hips together against the floor, which is the foundation for every harder movement. The plate adds load so it keeps being useful.

  1. Lie on your back holding a plate with straight arms above your chest
  2. Press your lower back firmly into the floor
  3. Lift your shoulder blades and your legs a few centimetres off the ground
  4. Keep the arms overhead if you can do so without the back arching
  5. Hold for the set time, then lower your legs and shoulders together
ea_plate_hollow_hold

Plate Pinch Grip Side Bend

Abdominals

PurposeTrains the side of the trunk and the grip at the same time, which is exactly the combination that carrying something heavy in one hand demands. The pinch grip usually gives out first, and that is fine.

  1. Stand tall pinching a plate by its smooth face in one hand
  2. Put the other hand on your head and keep both shoulders facing forward
  3. Let the plate pull you sideways, bending slowly toward that side
  4. Go only as far as you can control without twisting
  5. Pull back upright with the opposite side, then switch hands
ea_plate_pinch_grip_side_bend

Plate Russian Twist

Abdominals

PurposeRotating while holding a leaned-back position works the sides of the stomach while the front holds you up. Move from the ribs, not the arms — swinging a plate side to side with the shoulders trains nothing.

  1. Sit on the floor with knees bent, holding a plate with both hands
  2. Lean back until you feel your stomach engage, keeping the back straight
  3. Lift your feet off the floor if you can hold the position
  4. Rotate your ribs to one side, bringing the plate beside your hip
  5. Turn through the middle to the other side, keeping the movement controlled
ea_plate_russian_twist

Plate Situp

Abdominals

PurposeA sit-up you can load, so the stomach keeps getting stronger instead of just doing more repetitions. Holding the plate at the chest keeps the weight close; holding it overhead makes it much harder.

  1. Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor
  2. Hold a plate against your chest with both hands
  3. Tuck your chin slightly and brace your stomach
  4. Curl up one part of the spine at a time until your torso is upright
  5. Lower slowly in the same order, resisting all the way down
ea_plate_situp

Plate Standing Twist

Abdominals

PurposeTurning under a light load while standing trains the trunk to rotate over stable hips. Keep it light and controlled — speed and heavy weight together is the combination that hurts backs in twisting movements.

  1. Stand with feet shoulder width apart holding a plate at chest height
  2. Push the plate out until your arms are almost straight
  3. Brace your stomach and keep your hips facing forward
  4. Rotate your ribs and the plate to one side as far as is comfortable
  5. Return through the middle and rotate to the other side
ea_plate_standing_twist

Plate Wood Chopper

Abdominals

PurposeA diagonal movement from low on one side to high on the other, which trains the trunk the way it works in throwing and swinging. Almost all gym work is straight up and down, and this is not.

  1. Stand with feet shoulder width apart, holding a plate with both hands
  2. Start with the plate low beside one hip, knees slightly bent
  3. Sweep it diagonally up and across to above the opposite shoulder
  4. Let your feet pivot and your hips turn as the plate travels
  5. Lower it slowly along the same line, then do the whole set on the other side
ea_plate_wood_chopper

Reverse Plank

Abdominals

PurposeThe opposite of a normal plank: it loads the back of the body — glutes, hamstrings and the muscles between the shoulder blades. A direct counter to a day spent folded forward at a desk.

  1. Sit on the floor with your legs straight and your hands behind your hips, fingers forward
  2. Press through your hands and heels to lift your hips off the floor
  3. Squeeze your glutes until your body forms a straight line from heels to shoulders
  4. Open your chest and pull your shoulders down away from your ears
  5. Hold for the set time, breathing steadily, then lower under control
ea_reverse_plank elbowwrist

Barbell Coan Deadlift

Back

PurposeA deadlift done with the hips set higher and the bar dragged close, which shifts the work onto the upper back and hamstrings. It is a strength-sport variation — take it up only once a normal deadlift is comfortable and repeatable.

  1. Stand with the bar over your mid-foot, feet about hip width apart
  2. Grip the bar just outside your knees and set your hips higher than in a normal deadlift
  3. Pull the slack out of the bar and lock your upper back tight before anything moves
  4. Push the floor away and drag the bar up your shins, keeping it touching your legs
  5. Stand fully upright, then lower along the same path without rounding your back
ea_barbell_coan_deadlift hiplower_back

Barbell Reverse Deadlift

Back

PurposeStarting from the top and lowering first teaches the hip hinge without the hardest part — breaking the bar off the floor. Good for learning the movement and for loading the lowering phase, where most of the muscle is built.

  1. Set the bar in a rack at hip height and take it with an overhand grip, standing tall
  2. Push your hips back and let the bar slide down the front of your thighs
  3. Keep your back flat and your shins upright as the bar passes your knees
  4. Lower until you feel a strong stretch behind the thighs, then touch the floor if you can reach it
  5. Drive your hips forward to stand back up, finishing tall without leaning back
ea_barbell_reverse_deadlift hiplower_back

Barbell Zercher Good Morning

Back

PurposeHolding the bar in the crooks of your elbows puts the load in front of you, so the whole back has to work far harder to keep you from folding. Brutal for the upper back and the brace, and it teaches an honest hinge fast.

  1. Set the bar in a rack at stomach height and hook it into the crooks of both elbows
  2. Stand up with the bar held tight against your body, feet shoulder width apart
  3. Take a deep breath and lock your upper back and stomach
  4. Push your hips back and lower your chest toward the floor with the back flat
  5. Stop when your torso is near parallel, then drive the hips forward to stand
ea_barbell_zercher_good_morning hiplower_backupper_back

Cable Lat Prayer

Back

PurposeIsolates the lats with the arms nearly straight, so the biceps cannot take over the way they do on every row and pulldown. This is the exercise for people who pull a lot and still never feel their back working.

  1. Set a rope on the high pulley and kneel a step back from the machine
  2. Take both ends overhead with the arms almost straight and a small bend in the elbows
  3. Sit your hips back slightly and lengthen through the spine
  4. Pull the rope down in a wide arc toward your thighs without bending the elbows further
  5. Let the arms rise slowly back overhead until you feel the lats stretch
ea_cable_lat_prayer

Cable Pull in Kneeling

Back

PurposeKneeling removes the legs, so you cannot lean away and turn a row into a whole-body pull. What is left is the back, working against a cable that keeps its tension all the way to the stretch.

  1. Set a handle at chest height and kneel facing the machine, one step back
  2. Take the handle in both hands with the arms straight in front of you
  3. Squeeze your glutes and stomach so your body stays upright and still
  4. Pull the handle to your ribs, leading with the elbows and drawing the shoulder blades together
  5. Let the cable straighten your arms slowly, feeling the back stretch at the end
ea_cable_pull_in_kneeling knee

Cable Silverback Shrug

Back

PurposeA shrug done leaning forward against a cable, which points the work at the middle traps between the shoulder blades rather than the tops of the shoulders. That middle section is what holds your posture up all day.

  1. Set two handles at about hip height and stand facing the machine holding one in each hand
  2. Step back and lean forward from the hips with your back flat and arms hanging
  3. Let the cables pull your shoulder blades apart at the start of each rep
  4. Squeeze the shoulder blades together and slightly down, keeping the arms straight
  5. Hold the squeeze for a second, then let the blades open again under control
ea_cable_silverback_shrug lower_backupper_back

Dumbbell Alternating Pendlay Row

Back

PurposeEach rep starts from the floor with no momentum carried over, so the back has to produce the whole pull from a standstill. Alternating arms lets you hold the bent-over position longer without your lower back giving out first.

  1. Stand with feet hip width and hinge forward until your torso is nearly parallel to the floor
  2. Set two dumbbells on the floor directly under your shoulders and take one in each hand
  3. Keep your back flat and your neck in line with your spine
  4. Row one dumbbell to your ribs, then lower it fully to the floor and let it rest
  5. Row the other side the same way, alternating and resetting on the floor every rep
ea_dumbbell_alternating_pendlay_row lower_backupper_back

Dumbbell Goblet Good Morning

Back

PurposeThe gentlest way to learn the hip hinge — the movement underneath every deadlift, swing and row. Holding a weight at the chest gives you something to counterbalance against, so the pattern is easier to feel than with a bar on the back.

  1. Hold one dumbbell vertically against your chest with both hands, feet shoulder width apart
  2. Soften your knees slightly and keep them there
  3. Push your hips straight back as if closing a door behind you
  4. Lower your chest until you feel a stretch behind your thighs, back flat throughout
  5. Squeeze your glutes to drive the hips forward and stand tall
ea_dumbbell_goblet_good_morning hiplower_backupper_back

Dumbbell Knee Lawnmower Row

Back

PurposePulling on a diagonal from a low knee to the ribs works the back the way you actually use it — with some rotation, not in a straight line. It builds the connection between the lat and the opposite hip that carries into throwing and swinging.

  1. Take a staggered stance with one foot forward and rest the free hand on that thigh
  2. Hold a dumbbell in the other hand and let it hang toward the inside of the front foot
  3. Hinge forward with a flat back so the weight starts low and across your body
  4. Pull the dumbbell up and back toward your ribs, letting the torso open slightly
  5. Reverse the path slowly to the low starting point, then finish the set and switch sides
ea_dumbbell_knee_lawnmower_row upper_back

Dumbbell Pendlay Row

Back

PurposeResetting on the floor between every rep removes the bounce, so each pull is pure back strength from a dead stop. It carries over directly to the first inch of a deadlift, which is where most people are weakest.

  1. Hinge forward until your torso is roughly parallel to the floor, knees slightly bent
  2. Place both dumbbells on the floor under your shoulders
  3. Take a breath, brace, and keep your torso completely still for the whole rep
  4. Pull both dumbbells explosively to your ribs, elbows driving back
  5. Lower them all the way to the floor, let them settle, then pull again
ea_dumbbell_pendlay_row lower_backupper_back

Kettlebell Gorilla Row

Back

PurposeTwo bells on the floor let one side stay planted while the other rows, so you get a heavy back pull plus an anti-rotation job for the stomach. The wide stance keeps your lower back out of it more than a standard bent-over row does.

  1. Stand with feet wider than shoulder width and a kettlebell between your feet on each side
  2. Hinge at the hips with a flat back until you can grip both handles
  3. Push one bell into the floor to anchor yourself
  4. Row the other bell to your hip, keeping your shoulders level and your back flat
  5. Lower it to the floor and row the opposite side, alternating for the whole set
ea_kettlebell_gorilla_row upper_back

Kettlebell Pullover

Back

PurposeOne of the few movements that stretches the lats under load with the arms overhead. It opens the shoulders and the upper back, which is exactly what tightens up in anyone who sits at a desk.

  1. Lie on a bench or the floor and hold one kettlebell by the horns with both hands over your chest
  2. Keep a slight bend in the elbows and press your lower back into the surface
  3. Lower the bell back over your head in an arc, only as far as your shoulders allow
  4. Stop when you feel the stretch under the armpits, without your ribs flaring up
  5. Pull the bell back over your chest using the back, not the arms
ea_kettlebell_pullover shoulder

Kettlebell Row

Back

PurposeThe basic back builder with two bells: the handles sit low, so the range is longer than with dumbbells and the lats get more stretch at the bottom of each pull.

  1. Stand with feet hip width and a kettlebell just outside each foot
  2. Hinge forward with a flat back until your torso is close to parallel with the floor
  3. Grip both handles and let your arms hang straight down
  4. Row both bells to your ribs, driving the elbows back and squeezing the shoulder blades
  5. Lower under control until the arms are straight again, without rounding your back
ea_kettlebell_row upper_back

Kettlebell Single Arm Row

Back

PurposeOne arm at a time gives the shoulder blade room to travel further, so each lat gets a longer range than a two-handed row allows. It also shows you plainly which side is weaker.

  1. Place one hand and the same-side knee on a bench, with the other foot on the floor
  2. Hold the kettlebell in the free hand and let it hang straight down
  3. Set your back flat and your shoulders square to the floor
  4. Pull the bell to your hip, letting the shoulder blade slide toward your spine
  5. Lower it fully, allowing the blade to reach forward at the bottom, then change sides
ea_kettlebell_single_arm_row upper_back

Kipping Pull Up

Back

PurposeA pull-up that uses a hip swing to help the arms, which lets you do far more repetitions for conditioning. It trains rhythm and grip endurance rather than pure back strength — do strict pull-ups first, and only kip once you have them.

  1. Hang from the bar with an overhand grip, hands just outside shoulder width
  2. Swing your body into an arch and then a hollow position, driven from the shoulders
  3. As you swing forward, drive your knees and hips up to give the pull momentum
  4. Pull your chin over the bar at the top of that surge, elbows finishing behind you
  5. Fall back into the swing and let the next arch start the following repetition
ea_kipping_pull_up elbowshoulder

Landmine Romanian Deadlift

Back

PurposeThe landmine's arc keeps the bar travelling close to your legs by itself, so the hinge is harder to do badly than with a free bar. A good bridge for anyone whose back is nervous about conventional deadlifts.

  1. Load one end of a barbell in the landmine and straddle it, facing away from the anchor
  2. Reach down and hold the loaded end with both hands between your legs
  3. Stand tall with a small bend in the knees, back flat, shoulders down
  4. Push your hips back and let the bar travel down its arc close to your legs
  5. Stop at a strong hamstring stretch, then drive the hips forward to stand
ea_landmine_romanian_deadlift hiplower_back

Lawnmower Row

Back

PurposeNamed for the motion of starting a mower, and useful for the same reason: it trains a pull that involves the whole body turning slightly, which is how you actually pull things in life rather than in a gym.

  1. Stand in a split stance with a dumbbell in the hand opposite your front foot
  2. Rest your free hand on the front thigh and hinge forward with a flat back
  3. Let the dumbbell hang low and slightly across your body
  4. Pull it up past your ribs while opening the chest toward the working side
  5. Lower it slowly back across the body, then finish the set and switch sides
ea_lawnmower_row upper_back

Plate Alternating Deadstop Row

Back

PurposeEvery rep starts from a full stop on the floor, so nothing is carried over from the last one — the back does all of it. Alternating sides keeps the total time bent over manageable.

  1. Set two plates on their edges on the floor and stand between them, feet hip width
  2. Hinge forward with a flat back and grip the top edge of each plate
  3. Brace your stomach and keep your torso still throughout
  4. Row one plate to your ribs, then set it back down completely
  5. Row the other side the same way, pausing on the floor between every repetition
ea_plate_alternating_deadstop_row upper_back

Plate Glute Bridge to Pullover

Back

PurposeHolds the hips up with the glutes while the lats work overhead, so the front of your body is stretched open at both ends. A useful counter to a day spent folded forward at a desk.

  1. Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat, holding a plate over your chest
  2. Lift your hips into a bridge and keep the glutes squeezed for the whole set
  3. With slightly bent arms, lower the plate back over your head toward the floor
  4. Go only as far as you can without your ribs lifting or your hips dropping
  5. Pull the plate back over your chest using the lats, keeping the bridge held
ea_plate_glute_bridge_to_pullover hipshoulder

Plate Good Morning

Back

PurposeTeaches the hip hinge with a load you can hold anywhere, which makes it the version to practise at home. Holding the plate at the chest rather than a bar on the back keeps the spine loaded far more gently.

  1. Hold a weight plate against your chest with both hands, feet shoulder width apart
  2. Soften the knees and set your back flat
  3. Push your hips straight back and lower your chest toward the floor
  4. Keep the plate glued to your chest and your neck in line with your spine
  5. Stop at a strong stretch behind the thighs, then squeeze the glutes to stand
ea_plate_good_morning hiplower_backupper_back

Plate Pinch Grip Deadlift

Back

PurposePinching two plates between the fingers and thumb trains a grip that a hook or a strap can never build. Grip is the first thing to fail on heavy rows, carries and pull-ups, so it is worth training on its own.

  1. Stand two plates together on the floor with the smooth sides facing outward
  2. Stand over them with your feet either side, hips back and back flat
  3. Pinch the outer faces with your fingers and thumb — no hooking the rim
  4. Stand up by driving through the legs, keeping the plates hanging still
  5. Hold at the top for a few seconds, then lower under control before your grip fails
ea_plate_pinch_grip_deadlift hiplower_back

Plate Pinch Grip Row

Back

PurposeA back row and a grip test in one: the pinch hold fails long before the back does, so every rep is fighting to keep hold. Best used late in a session when heavy rowing is already done.

  1. Hinge forward with a flat back, holding a plate pinched in each hand by its smooth face
  2. Let both plates hang straight down under your shoulders
  3. Brace your stomach and hold the torso still
  4. Row both plates to your ribs, keeping the pinch tight
  5. Lower them slowly to arms' length and repeat until the grip, not the back, stops you
ea_plate_pinch_grip_row upper_back

Push Pull Chair Over Head Pull

Back

PurposePulling a loaded sled with the rope overhead works the lats and the whole back without any lowering phase, so you can add hard back work without the soreness that limits how often you train.

  1. Attach a rope to the sled and sit or stand facing it at the far end
  2. Take the rope with both hands and raise your arms overhead, arms straight
  3. Set your feet and brace so your torso stays upright
  4. Pull the rope down and back past your head, hand over hand, drawing the sled toward you
  5. Reach forward for the next grip and keep pulling until the sled reaches you
ea_push_pull_chair_over_head_pull

Seated Row Machine Rows

Back

PurposeThe machine supports your chest and lower back, so you can pull heavy without your spine having to hold the position. This is usually the safest heavy row available, and the one to choose when the lower back is already tired.

  1. Set the seat height so the handles line up with the middle of your chest
  2. Sit with your chest against the pad and your feet planted
  3. Take the handles with your arms straight and shoulder blades relaxed forward
  4. Pull the handles to your ribs, driving the elbows back and squeezing the blades together
  5. Return slowly until the arms are straight and the blades open again
ea_seated_row_machine_rows upper_back

Straight Arm Cable Lat Pull Down

Back

PurposeWith the elbows locked the biceps cannot contribute, so the lats do the entire pull. It is the standard fix for a back workout you feel everywhere except your back.

  1. Attach a straight bar to the high pulley and stand a step back, feet hip width
  2. Take the bar with an overhand grip and straight arms at about head height
  3. Hinge forward slightly at the hips and keep your back flat
  4. Sweep the bar down in an arc to your thighs without bending the elbows
  5. Let the bar rise back slowly to head height, feeling the stretch under the arms
ea_straight_arm_cable_lat_pull_down

Suspension Trainer with Grips Wide Grip Inverted Row on Floor_1

Back

PurposeA row where your own body is the weight, so you can make it as easy or as hard as you need just by moving your feet. The wide grip aims the work at the upper back and rear shoulders, the muscles that pull the shoulders back.

  1. Set the straps so the handles hang at about hip height and take one in each hand
  2. Walk your feet forward and lean back until your arms are straight and your body is a straight line
  3. Set your hands wider than your shoulders with palms facing down
  4. Pull your chest to the handles, driving the elbows out and back and squeezing the blades
  5. Lower under control to straight arms, keeping your hips from sagging
ea_suspension_trainer_with_grips_wide_grip_inverted_row_on_floor_1 upper_back

Theraband Scapula Retraction

Back

PurposeA light movement for the muscles between the shoulder blades, which get long and weak from hours at a keyboard. Doing it often matters more than doing it heavy — it is a posture exercise, not a strength one.

  1. Hold a light band with both hands at chest height, arms straight in front of you
  2. Stand tall with your ribs down and your chin gently tucked
  3. Keep your arms straight and pull the band apart by drawing your shoulder blades together
  4. Squeeze for two seconds at the point where your chest opens fully
  5. Return slowly to the start without letting your shoulders creep up toward your ears
ea_theraband_scapula_retraction upper_back

Weighted Back Extensions on Hyperextension Bench

Back

PurposeTrains the muscles that run along the spine to hold a position under load — the exact job they do during a deadlift or a heavy carry. A strong set of these is one of the better insurances against a back that gives out.

  1. Set the pad just below your hip bones and hook your heels under the rollers
  2. Hold a plate against your chest and cross your arms over it
  3. Start folded forward at the hips with your back flat, not rounded
  4. Squeeze your glutes and lift your torso until your body forms a straight line
  5. Stop there — do not arch past straight — and lower slowly under control
ea_weighted_back_extensions_on_hyperextension_bench lower_back

Alternate Biceps Curl Resistance Band

Biceps

PurposeWorks one arm at a time so the stronger side cannot quietly take over, which is what happens on every two-handed curl. A band keeps tension on the biceps at the top of the movement, where a dumbbell goes light and the muscle gets a rest it did not earn.

  1. Stand on the middle of the band with feet hip width apart and hold one end in each hand, palms forward
  2. Keep your elbows pinned against your ribs and your shoulders down
  3. Curl one hand up toward the shoulder, letting the band stretch, and keep the other arm straight
  4. Lower that hand under control all the way down before the other arm starts
  5. Alternate arms for the whole set, never letting the elbows drift forward
ea_alternate_biceps_curl_resistance_band elbow

Alternate Biceps Curl Standing Dumbbells

Biceps

PurposeThe plainest way to build the biceps and the one every other curl is measured against. Alternating halves the load on your torso at any moment, so you can stand upright and let the arm do the work instead of swinging the weight up with your back.

  1. Stand tall with a dumbbell in each hand, arms straight down, palms facing forward
  2. Brace your stomach and keep your elbows touching your sides
  3. Curl the right dumbbell up to shoulder height, keeping the wrist straight
  4. Lower it slowly to the bottom, then curl the left one the same way
  5. Keep your back still — if your shoulders rock, the weight is too heavy
ea_alternate_biceps_curl_standing_dumbbells elbow

Cable Twisting Biceps Curl

Biceps

PurposeTurning the palm outward as you curl is what the biceps actually does — it bends the elbow and rotates the forearm, and most curls only ask for half of that. The cable holds tension through the whole path, including the turn, which a free weight cannot do.

  1. Set a single handle on the lowest pulley and stand facing the machine, one step back
  2. Take the handle with your palm facing your thigh and let your arm hang straight
  3. Curl upward and rotate your palm to face the ceiling as the elbow bends
  4. Finish with the hand at shoulder height and the palm fully turned up, elbow still at your side
  5. Reverse both movements slowly — unbend and untwist together — then repeat
ea_cable_twisting_biceps_curl elbow

Dumbbell Seated Zottman Curl

Biceps

PurposeOne exercise that trains both sides of the arm: you lift with the palm up, which loads the biceps, and lower with the palm down, which loads the forearm. Sitting removes the leg drive, so nothing but the arms moves the weight.

  1. Sit on the end of a bench with a dumbbell in each hand, arms hanging, palms forward
  2. Curl both dumbbells up to your shoulders with your elbows fixed at your sides
  3. At the top, rotate your wrists so the palms now face the floor
  4. Lower the dumbbells slowly in that position — this half should feel harder and take longer
  5. At the bottom, rotate the palms forward again and start the next repetition
ea_dumbbell_seated_zottman_curl elbow

Kettlebell Concentration Curl

Biceps

PurposeBracing the elbow against the inside of the thigh removes every way of cheating — you cannot swing, lean back or shrug the weight up. What is left is the biceps alone, which is why this is the exercise people use when an arm is visibly lagging.

  1. Sit on a bench with your feet wide and lean forward slightly from the hips
  2. Hold the kettlebell in one hand and brace the back of that upper arm against the inside of the same thigh
  3. Let the arm hang straight down so the bell is just off the floor
  4. Curl the bell up toward your shoulder without letting the elbow leave the thigh
  5. Lower all the way until the arm is straight, then repeat and switch sides
ea_kettlebell_concentration_curl elbow

Kettlebell Curl

Biceps

PurposeThe bell hangs below your hand rather than sitting in it, so the weight pulls the wrist backwards the whole way up. Your forearm has to work to keep the wrist straight, which is grip training you get for free alongside the biceps.

  1. Stand with a kettlebell in each hand, handles gripped so the bells hang in front of your thighs
  2. Keep your wrists straight and locked — do not let the bells bend them back
  3. Curl both bells up toward your shoulders with the elbows against your sides
  4. Stop when your forearms are vertical and the bells rest against your forearms
  5. Lower under control to full arm extension before the next repetition
ea_kettlebell_curl elbow

Kettlebell Goblet Curl

Biceps

PurposeHolding one bell with both hands keeps the load exactly in front of your chest, so a single heavy weight can be curled without either wrist twisting out of line. It is the simplest way to add load when two lighter bells are all you have.

  1. Stand tall and hold one kettlebell by the horns with both hands, arms hanging in front of you
  2. Keep the bell upside down or upright — whichever lets both wrists stay straight
  3. Press your elbows into your ribs and brace your stomach
  4. Curl the bell up to chest height using only the elbows
  5. Lower slowly all the way down without letting your body lean back
ea_kettlebell_goblet_curl elbow

Kettlebell Preacher Curl

Biceps

PurposeThe pad under your arm stops the elbow from travelling, which is the one thing that lets the shoulder help on a standing curl. With that route closed the biceps has to finish the lift from the hardest position — arm nearly straight.

  1. Set the preacher bench so the top of the pad sits under your armpit when you sit down
  2. Lay the back of one upper arm flat along the pad and hold the kettlebell in that hand
  3. Straighten the arm until you feel the stretch, but do not let the elbow lock hard
  4. Curl the bell up toward your shoulder, keeping the arm glued to the pad
  5. Lower slowly to the stretched position and repeat, then change arms
ea_kettlebell_preacher_curl elbow

Kettlebell Single Arm Curl

Biceps

PurposeOne arm at a time exposes the difference between your sides, which a two-handed curl always hides. Working the weaker arm to the same number of clean repetitions is how that gap actually closes.

  1. Stand with your feet hip width apart and a kettlebell hanging in one hand
  2. Put the free hand on your hip so you can feel if your torso starts to lean
  3. Curl the bell up toward the shoulder with the elbow fixed at your side
  4. Lower it under control until the arm is fully straight
  5. Finish all repetitions on that arm, then match the same number on the other side
ea_kettlebell_single_arm_curl elbow

Landmine Bicep Curl

Biceps

PurposeThe bar swings on a fixed arc, so the resistance changes as you rise and the top of the curl stays heavy instead of going weightless. Both hands share one bar, which lets you load more than a pair of dumbbells you can control.

  1. Load one end of a barbell in the landmine holder and stand facing it
  2. Pick up the loaded end with both hands cupped underneath it, arms straight
  3. Stand tall with elbows against your ribs and the bar resting in your palms
  4. Curl the end of the bar up toward your chin, following the arc it wants to travel
  5. Lower slowly along the same arc until your arms are straight again
ea_landmine_bicep_curl elbow

Landmine Concentration Curl

Biceps

PurposeCombines the elbow brace of a concentration curl with the landmine's changing resistance, so the hardest part lands near the top rather than halfway. Useful when a dumbbell concentration curl has stopped feeling like anything.

  1. Set a barbell in the landmine and sit or half-kneel beside the loaded end
  2. Grip the end of the bar in one hand and brace that upper arm against the inside of your thigh
  3. Let the arm hang so the bar is at its lowest point
  4. Curl the bar up toward the shoulder, keeping the elbow pressed into the thigh
  5. Lower under control to a straight arm, then repeat and switch sides
ea_landmine_concentration_curl elbow

Plate Curl to Overhead Press

Biceps

PurposeTwo movements on one breath: the curl builds the arms, the press builds the shoulders, and the plate held out in front makes your stomach work to stop you leaning back. A whole upper body in one exercise when a single plate is all the equipment you have.

  1. Hold a weight plate at the sides with both hands, arms hanging in front of your hips
  2. Curl the plate up to chest height, keeping your elbows close to your body
  3. From there press it straight overhead until your arms lock out
  4. Lower the plate back to your chest with control
  5. Uncurl it down to your hips — that is one repetition
ea_plate_curl_to_overhead_press elbowshoulder

Reverse Curl Barbell

Biceps

PurposeTurning the palms down shifts the work off the biceps and onto the muscle underneath it and the top of the forearm — the two things that decide how thick the arm looks from the side and how long your grip lasts.

  1. Take a barbell with an overhand grip, hands about shoulder width apart
  2. Stand tall with the bar resting against your thighs and elbows at your sides
  3. Curl the bar up toward your chest without letting the wrists bend backwards
  4. Stop when your forearms are vertical, keeping the knuckles pointing up
  5. Lower slowly to the thighs — expect to use noticeably less weight than a normal curl
ea_reverse_curl_barbell elbowwrist

180 Jump Turns

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeJumping and landing after a half turn trains the legs to absorb force while the body is rotating, which is when ankles and knees are most vulnerable. Practising it deliberately is cheaper than learning it by accident.

  1. Stand with your feet hip width apart and your knees slightly bent
  2. Swing your arms back and dip into a quarter squat
  3. Jump up and turn one hundred and eighty degrees in the air
  4. Land softly on both feet with the knees bent and tracking over the toes
  5. Pause, reset, then jump back the other way
ea_180_jump_turns ankleknee

Agility Ladder Advanced Hop Position

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeTrains the feet to move accurately at speed, which is what separates quick from merely fast. The ladder gives immediate feedback — if your feet are sloppy, you catch a rung.

  1. Stand at one end of the ladder with your feet together and knees soft
  2. Hop with both feet into the first square, landing on the balls of the feet
  3. Immediately hop forward into the next square without pausing
  4. Keep your chest up and use your arms to help the rhythm
  5. Work the length of the ladder, then walk back and repeat
ea_agility_ladder_advanced_hop_position ankleknee

Agility Ladder Advanced Single-leg

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeHopping on one leg through the ladder builds the ankle stability that stops a rolled ankle when you land awkwardly. It also shows immediately which leg is less controlled.

  1. Stand on one leg at the end of the ladder with the knee slightly bent
  2. Hop forward into the first square, landing on the ball of that foot
  3. Absorb the landing through the ankle and knee before the next hop
  4. Continue down the ladder without putting the other foot down
  5. Walk back and repeat on the other leg
ea_agility_ladder_advanced_single_leg

Agility Ladder Advancing Laterally Switching Base

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeMoving sideways while changing which foot leads trains the pattern used every time you shuffle to cover ground in a sport. Almost nothing in a normal gym session works this direction.

  1. Stand side-on at one end of the ladder with your knees bent
  2. Step the lead foot into the first square, then follow with the other
  3. Step the lead foot out the far side, then bring the other out too
  4. Switch which foot leads and continue moving sideways down the ladder
  5. Work back the other way so both directions get equal time
ea_agility_ladder_advancing_laterally_switching_base

Agility Ladder Lateral Movement in in Out

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeA three-count sideways pattern, which forces you to change the leading foot repeatedly instead of settling into one rhythm. That constant switching is closer to how sport actually moves.

  1. Stand side-on at the end of the ladder with your weight on the balls of your feet
  2. Step the lead foot in, then the trail foot in
  3. Step the lead foot out the far side while the trail foot stays
  4. Continue this three-count rhythm while travelling sideways
  5. Repeat facing the other way so both sides lead
ea_agility_ladder_lateral_movement_in_in_out

Agility Ladder Lateral Movement with Double Hop

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeTwo-footed hops travelling sideways train the legs to load and release quickly from a stable base. It builds the elastic quality that makes changing direction feel light rather than laboured.

  1. Stand side-on at the end of the ladder with the feet together
  2. Hop sideways into the first square with both feet at once
  3. Hop again immediately into the next square without a pause
  4. Land on the balls of the feet and keep the knees soft throughout
  5. Travel the whole ladder, then work back leading with the other side
ea_agility_ladder_lateral_movement_with_double_hop ankleknee

Agility Ladder Skipping 1 Touch

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeOne touch per square at speed is the simplest ladder drill and the best for building pure foot speed. Everything else on a ladder is a variation on being able to do this cleanly.

  1. Stand at the end of the ladder on the balls of your feet
  2. Run forward placing one foot in each square, one touch per square
  3. Keep your steps short, quick and light
  4. Pump your arms in time with your feet
  5. Sprint the length of the ladder, walk back, and repeat
ea_agility_ladder_skipping_1_touch

Agility Ladder Skipping 2 Touches

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeTwo touches per square doubles the number of foot contacts, which is where foot speed is actually built. Harder to keep clean than one touch, and that difficulty is the point.

  1. Stand at the end of the ladder with your knees soft
  2. Run forward placing both feet inside each square before moving on
  3. Keep the contacts light and the rhythm even
  4. Stay tall with your chest up and your arms driving
  5. Work the full length, then walk back and go again
ea_agility_ladder_skipping_2_touches

Agility Ladder in in Out Out

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeThe foundational ladder pattern: two feet in, two feet out, repeated at speed. It teaches the feet to move in a rhythm the brain does not have to think about, which is what frees attention up in a game.

  1. Stand at the end of the ladder facing down its length
  2. Step the left foot into the first square, then the right
  3. Step the left foot out to the left of the next square, then the right out to the right
  4. Keep the rhythm even: in, in, out, out
  5. Move down the whole ladder, then walk back and repeat
ea_agility_ladder_in_in_out_out

Agility Ladder in in Out Out Moving Laterally

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeThe same in-in-out-out rhythm travelling sideways, which adds a direction almost no other training covers. Sideways speed is what most people lack, and it is trainable.

  1. Stand side-on at the end of the ladder with your knees bent and chest up
  2. Step the near foot into the square, then the far foot in beside it
  3. Step the near foot out the other side, then the far foot out
  4. Keep travelling sideways with the same four-count rhythm
  5. Return down the ladder leading with the other side
ea_agility_ladder_in_in_out_out_moving_laterally

Agility Ladder in in Out Out with Knee Lift

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeAdding a knee lift raises the demand on the hip flexors and on balance, so it becomes a conditioning drill as well as a footwork one. Good near the end of a warm-up when the heart rate should already be up.

  1. Stand at the end of the ladder with your feet hip width apart
  2. Step both feet into the first square in quick succession
  3. As you step out to the sides, drive one knee up toward your chest
  4. Land and repeat, alternating which knee lifts each time
  5. Work the length of the ladder, then walk back and go again
ea_agility_ladder_in_in_out_out_with_knee_lift

Air Swing Running

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeSupporting your bodyweight on the bars while running in the air loads the shoulders and stomach continuously while the legs move. It builds the ability to hold a position while something else is happening.

  1. Grip the dip bars and press up until your arms are straight
  2. Push your shoulders down away from your ears and brace your stomach
  3. Keeping the arms locked, drive one knee up toward your chest
  4. Switch legs in a running rhythm without letting your body swing
  5. Continue for the set time, then lower down under control
ea_air_swing_running anklehipkneelower_back

Air Swing Side to Side Swing

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeSwinging the legs side to side while supported trains the stomach to control rotation, and the shoulders to stay solid while the load moves. Control matters far more than how far the legs travel.

  1. Support yourself on the dip bars with your arms straight and shoulders down
  2. Bring both legs together and brace your stomach hard
  3. Swing both legs slowly to one side, keeping your torso still
  4. Control the swing back through the middle to the other side
  5. Continue for the set time without letting the shoulders shrug
ea_air_swing_side_to_side_swing hiplower_back

Air Swing Walking

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeThe slowest of the supported leg movements, which makes it the place to start. Holding the support position itself is most of the benefit — the walking just keeps the stomach honest.

  1. Press up on the dip bars until your arms are locked straight
  2. Set your shoulders down and away from your ears
  3. Lift one knee slowly and lower it, then the other
  4. Keep the rhythm slow and deliberate, with no swinging
  5. Continue for the set time, then step or lower down
ea_air_swing_walking hiplower_back

Arms Lateral Raise and Rotation Up

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeA warm-up that takes the shoulder through its full range with no load, which is exactly what it needs before pressing. Two minutes of this changes how the first heavy set feels.

  1. Stand tall with your arms hanging by your sides
  2. Raise both arms out to the sides until they are level with your shoulders
  3. Rotate the palms to face upward, then continue lifting overhead
  4. Reach as high as the shoulders comfortably allow
  5. Reverse the whole path slowly and repeat for the set
ea_arms_lateral_raise_and_rotation_up hipshoulderwrist

Ball Slams

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeThrowing a ball into the ground as hard as you can trains the whole body to produce force fast, and it is one of the few exercises where you can go completely all out safely. Also a very effective way to raise the heart rate.

  1. Stand with your feet shoulder width apart holding the ball at your chest
  2. Raise the ball overhead, extending fully onto your toes
  3. Brace your stomach and slam the ball down into the floor as hard as you can
  4. Follow through by hinging at the hips, keeping your back flat
  5. Pick the ball up and repeat immediately for the set
ea_ball_slams

Band Squat Row

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposePuts a squat and a row into one movement, so legs and back are trained together and the heart rate stays up. A whole workout in one exercise when all you have is a band.

  1. Anchor a band at chest height and hold an end in each hand, stepping back until it is tight
  2. Stand with your feet shoulder width apart and your arms straight
  3. Squat down until your thighs are about parallel to the floor
  4. As you stand back up, pull both hands to your ribs, squeezing the shoulder blades
  5. Extend the arms as you sink into the next squat
ea_band_squat_row anklehipkneeupper_back

Barbell Jump Shrug

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeA partial version of the olympic pull that teaches the hips to extend explosively, without needing the technique a full clean demands. It is the most accessible way to train real power with a barbell.

  1. Stand holding a barbell at arm's length in front of your thighs, feet hip width
  2. Push your hips back until the bar is just above your knees, back flat
  3. Drive your hips forward violently and extend your legs
  4. Shrug your shoulders hard at the top and rise onto your toes
  5. Let the bar lower back to the start and reset before the next repetition
ea_barbell_jump_shrug anklekneelower_backneckupper_back

Battle Rope Alternating Arm Waves

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeRaises the heart rate hard while putting almost no impact through the joints, which makes it useful for conditioning when knees or ankles are sore. The shoulders and stomach work continuously.

  1. Hold one rope end in each hand and stand facing the anchor point
  2. Set your feet shoulder width apart and sink into a quarter squat
  3. Brace your stomach and keep your chest up
  4. Whip one arm up and down, then the other, creating alternating waves
  5. Keep the rhythm fast and continuous for the set time
ea_battle_rope_alternating_arm_waves

Battle Rope Double Arm Slams

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeBoth arms together means the whole body has to produce each wave, so this is closer to power work than the alternating version. Short, hard intervals suit it better than long sets.

  1. Hold one rope end in each hand, facing the anchor, feet shoulder width apart
  2. Raise both arms overhead, extending through your whole body
  3. Slam both rope ends down toward the floor at the same time
  4. Let your hips hinge back as the ropes come down, keeping the back flat
  5. Drive back up immediately and repeat for the set time
ea_battle_rope_double_arm_slams

Bear Crawls

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeCrawling on hands and feet with the knees just off the floor forces the stomach to hold the spine still while all four limbs move. It is a plank you travel in, and much harder than it looks.

  1. Start on hands and knees with wrists under shoulders
  2. Tuck your toes and lift your knees a few centimetres off the floor
  3. Keep your back flat and your hips low, roughly level with your shoulders
  4. Move the opposite hand and foot forward together, then the other pair
  5. Travel for the set distance keeping the hips from swaying side to side
ea_bear_crawls elbowwrist

Box Sled Push

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposePushing weight with no lowering phase means you can work extremely hard without the muscle damage that limits how often you train. The legs and lungs get everything; the next day costs nothing.

  1. Load the sled and grip the high handles or the frame
  2. Lean your body forward at about forty-five degrees with straight arms
  3. Keep your back flat and your head in line with your spine
  4. Drive through the balls of your feet with short powerful steps
  5. Push for the set distance, then rest fully before the next run
ea_box_sled_push

Crawl with Sled Drag

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeCombines a bear crawl with a load behind you, which turns a stomach exercise into full-body conditioning. Everything works at once, and it is over quickly, which is the appeal.

  1. Attach a harness or strap from the sled around your waist
  2. Get into a bear crawl position with knees just off the floor
  3. Keep your back flat and your hips low
  4. Crawl forward using opposite hand and foot together, dragging the sled behind
  5. Cover the set distance, then rest before the next round
ea_crawl_with_sled_drag

Double Kettlebell Sled Push

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposePushing with a bell in each hand adds a grip and shoulder demand to a leg drill, so more of the body is involved. Useful when there is no proper sled but there are kettlebells and a smooth floor.

  1. Place two kettlebells on the floor in front of you, handles forward
  2. Get into a low athletic position with your hands on the bells
  3. Keep your back flat and your arms firm
  4. Drive forward with short steps, pushing the bells along the floor
  5. Cover the set distance, then reset and repeat
ea_double_kettlebell_sled_push

Dumbbell Curl Press Extend

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeThree arm exercises chained without putting the weights down, so biceps, shoulders and triceps all get worked in one continuous set. Efficient when time is short and the weights are light.

  1. Stand tall with a dumbbell in each hand, arms by your sides
  2. Curl both dumbbells up to your shoulders
  3. Press them straight overhead until the arms lock out
  4. Bend the elbows to lower the weights behind your head, then extend back up
  5. Lower to the shoulders and down to your sides — that is one repetition
ea_dumbbell_curl_press_extend elbowkneeshoulderwrist

Dumbbell Swing

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeTrains the hips to snap open explosively, which is the foundation of jumping, sprinting and lifting anything quickly. The weight is moved by the hips, not lifted by the arms — that distinction is the whole exercise.

  1. Stand with feet slightly wider than your shoulders, a dumbbell held in both hands
  2. Push your hips back and let the weight swing between your legs, back flat
  3. Snap your hips forward hard and squeeze your glutes
  4. Let that force swing the dumbbell up to about chest height — do not lift it with your arms
  5. Let it fall back between the legs and go straight into the next repetition
ea_dumbbell_swing hiplower_back

Elbow-extension

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeA no-equipment movement for the back of the arm, useful as a warm-up before pressing or as a way to train the triceps when nothing is available. Light, and meant to be done for higher repetitions.

  1. Stand or sit tall with your upper arms raised beside your head
  2. Bend the elbows so your hands drop behind your neck
  3. Keep the upper arms still and pointing at the ceiling
  4. Straighten the elbows to extend your hands overhead, squeezing at the top
  5. Lower slowly and repeat for the set
ea_elbow_extension kneewrist

Front Lever Raise

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeOne of the hardest bodyweight pulls there is: the lats and stomach have to hold the whole body horizontal from a bar. Work through tucked and one-leg progressions first — the full version takes months.

  1. Hang from a bar with an overhand grip, arms straight and shoulders engaged
  2. Squeeze your glutes and stomach so the body is one rigid line
  3. Pull down on the bar with straight arms to raise your body toward horizontal
  4. Tuck the knees or extend one leg to reduce the difficulty as needed
  5. Lower under control back to the hang without swinging
ea_front_lever_raise hipshoulder

Front Lever Raise to Hold

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeAdds a static hold at the top of the raise, which is where the position is actually built. Holding is harder than passing through, and it is what turns the movement into strength rather than a trick.

  1. Hang from a bar with straight arms and an active shoulder position
  2. Brace your whole body into one rigid line
  3. Pull down with straight arms to raise your body toward horizontal
  4. Hold that position for as long as your line stays straight
  5. Lower slowly to the hang and rest fully before the next attempt
ea_front_lever_raise_to_hold hipshoulder

Gorilla Walk

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeMoving in a deep squat with the hands reaching the floor opens the hips while the legs work, which makes it a warm-up and a conditioning drill at once. It also builds squat depth by spending time there.

  1. Squat down deep with your feet wider than your shoulders
  2. Place both hands on the floor in front of you
  3. Keep your chest up and your heels down as much as you can
  4. Move sideways or forward by stepping the feet and then the hands
  5. Continue for the set distance, staying low the whole time
ea_gorilla_walk

Hand Stand Hold

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeBuilds shoulder strength and whole-body control in a way nothing else does, and it improves the sense of where your body is in space. Learn it against a wall first, and never on a hard floor without a plan for coming down.

  1. Place your hands on the floor about shoulder width apart, a foot from a wall
  2. Kick one leg up and then the other so your heels rest on the wall
  3. Push the floor away, lock your elbows and squeeze your glutes and stomach
  4. Stack your hips over your shoulders and look between your hands
  5. Hold for as long as your line stays straight, then come down one leg at a time
ea_hand_stand_hold

Headstand

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeAn inversion that builds neck, shoulder and stomach control, and gives the same sense of orientation a handstand does with far less strength required. Take the weight on the arms, never on the head.

  1. Kneel and place your forearms on the mat with the hands clasped
  2. Set the crown of your head on the floor with the back of it against your hands
  3. Press hard through the forearms so most of your weight is there, not on your head
  4. Walk your feet in and lift the hips over your shoulders, then raise the legs
  5. Hold with the body in one line, then lower one leg at a time under control
ea_headstand neck

Heavy Bag Sled Drag

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeDragging backwards loads the front of the thighs specifically, and because there is no lowering phase it is one of the few ways to train the knees hard without soreness. Often used in knee rehabilitation for exactly that reason.

  1. Attach a strap from the bag or sled and hold one end in each hand
  2. Face the load and lean back slightly with your arms straight
  3. Keep your chest up and your stomach braced
  4. Walk backwards with short steps, pulling the load toward you
  5. Cover the set distance, then reset and go again
ea_heavy_bag_sled_drag

Kettlebell Sled Drag

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeA sled substitute using what most gyms already have. Dragging trains the legs and grip with no lowering phase, so you can add a lot of work without adding recovery cost.

  1. Attach a strap or rope to a heavy kettlebell
  2. Hold the other end in one or both hands and stand facing away from the bell
  3. Lean forward slightly with your arms firm and your back flat
  4. Walk forward with short, deliberate steps, dragging the bell behind you
  5. Cover the set distance, then turn around and repeat
ea_kettlebell_sled_drag

Kettlebell Snatch

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeTakes the bell from the floor to overhead in one movement, which trains power and conditioning at the same time. Technically demanding — learn the swing properly first, because the snatch is a swing that keeps going.

  1. Stand with the bell on the floor between your feet and hinge to grip it with one hand
  2. Swing it back between your legs, then snap your hips forward hard
  3. Guide the bell up close to your body, keeping the arm relaxed
  4. As it passes your head, punch your hand through so the bell rotates around the wrist rather than banging it
  5. Lock the arm overhead, then guide the bell back down into the next swing
ea_kettlebell_snatch lower_backshoulderwrist

Kettlebell Turkish Get Up

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeGetting from lying to standing with a weight overhead trains shoulder stability, hip mobility and body control in one slow movement. It takes about half a minute per repetition, and it exposes every weak link you have.

  1. Lie on your back and press the bell overhead with one arm, that knee bent
  2. Roll onto the opposite forearm, then push up onto that hand
  3. Lift your hips and sweep the straight leg back into a kneeling position
  4. Bring your torso upright, then stand up, keeping the bell locked overhead throughout
  5. Reverse every step exactly to return to lying, then change arms
ea_kettlebell_turkish_get_up

Kettlebell Walkover Pushup

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeMoving a hand onto and off a kettlebell between push-ups adds a shoulder-stability and anti-rotation demand to a familiar movement. It also increases the depth on one side each repetition.

  1. Set a kettlebell on the floor and take a push-up position with one hand on it
  2. Keep your feet wide and your body in a straight line
  3. Lower into a push-up, then press back up
  4. Walk the free hand over the bell and swap which hand is on it
  5. Do another push-up and continue, alternating hands each repetition
ea_kettlebell_walkover_pushup

Kettlebell Windmill

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeHolding a weight overhead while bending sideways to the floor demands shoulder stability, hip mobility and trunk strength together. Start with no weight at all — the position is the hard part, not the load.

  1. Press a kettlebell overhead with one arm and turn both feet away from that side
  2. Keep your eyes on the bell and your arm locked straight
  3. Push your hips toward the loaded side and slide the free hand down your leg
  4. Lower until that hand reaches the floor or as far as you can with a straight back
  5. Return to standing along the same path, then finish the set and change sides
ea_kettlebell_windmill

Kipping Handstand Push-up

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeUses a knee drive to help the arms press, which allows far more repetitions than a strict handstand push-up. It trains conditioning and rhythm, not raw pressing strength — learn the strict version first.

  1. Kick up into a handstand with your heels resting against a wall
  2. Lower under control until the top of your head touches the floor or a pad
  3. Tuck your knees toward your chest
  4. Drive the knees up hard and press with the arms at the same moment
  5. Lock out overhead, reset your body line, and repeat
ea_kipping_handstand_push_up elbowneckshoulderwrist

Landmine Alternating Lunge and Twist

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeCombines a lunge with a rotation, so the legs work while the trunk turns under load. It trains the two things together, which is how the body actually moves outside a gym.

  1. Hold the loaded bar end at chest height with both hands, standing away from the anchor
  2. Step back into a reverse lunge with one leg
  3. As you lower, rotate your ribs toward the front leg
  4. Untwist as you drive through the front heel to stand
  5. Repeat on the other leg, alternating throughout the set
ea_landmine_alternating_lunge_and_twist hipkneewrist

Landmine Alternating Lunge to Chest Press

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeA lunge that finishes as a press, so the legs and the upper body are trained in one continuous movement. The heart rate rises quickly, which makes it a conditioning exercise as much as a strength one.

  1. Hold the loaded bar end at one shoulder, facing away from the anchor
  2. Step back into a reverse lunge until the back knee is near the floor
  3. Drive through the front heel to stand back up
  4. Press the bar forward and up to a straight arm as you finish standing
  5. Return it to the shoulder, switch sides, and repeat
ea_landmine_alternating_lunge_to_chest_press hipkneeshoulder

Landmine Rotational Lift to Press

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeTakes the bar from low on one side to overhead on the other, which trains the diagonal chain from the hip through the trunk to the shoulder. That chain is what produces force in throwing and striking.

  1. Stand side-on to the landmine and hold the loaded end low beside one hip
  2. Bend your knees slightly and brace your stomach
  3. Rotate and drive up through the hips, lifting the bar diagonally across your body
  4. Finish by pressing it overhead on the opposite side
  5. Reverse the path under control, then complete the set and change sides
ea_landmine_rotational_lift_to_press kneeshoulder

Lateral Sled Drag

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeDragging sideways loads the side of the hip, which almost no other loaded exercise reaches. That muscle is what keeps the knee tracking properly, and it is chronically undertrained.

  1. Attach a strap to the sled and hold it with both hands
  2. Stand side-on to the sled with your knees bent and chest up
  3. Keep your feet pointing forward, not toward the sled
  4. Step sideways with the lead foot and follow with the other, pulling the sled along
  5. Cover the set distance, then turn around and lead with the other side
ea_lateral_sled_drag

Low Box Lateral Runner

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeQuick sideways steps on and off a low box train the feet and the side of the hip to react fast. It raises the heart rate quickly and needs almost no space.

  1. Stand side-on beside a low box with your knees bent
  2. Step the near foot onto the box, then the other foot
  3. Step down on the far side, one foot at a time, without pausing
  4. Reverse immediately and travel back the other way
  5. Keep the contacts light and quick for the set time
ea_low_box_lateral_runner

Low Box Quick Feet

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeTapping the box as fast as possible trains pure foot speed and the ability to change contact quickly. It is short, simple, and one of the best things to do at the end of a warm-up.

  1. Stand facing a low box with your knees slightly bent
  2. Tap the top of the box with the ball of one foot
  3. Swap feet as fast as you can, alternating taps
  4. Stay on the balls of your feet and keep your chest up
  5. Work for fifteen to twenty seconds, then rest and repeat
ea_low_box_quick_feet

Low Rotational Med Ball Chops (quarter Squat, Rotating Med Ball Left and Ride Across Core)

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeRotating a ball across the body from a quarter squat trains the trunk to turn while the legs hold a position. That combination is what every throwing and striking movement is built on.

  1. Hold a medicine ball with both hands and sink into a quarter squat
  2. Keep your chest up and your stomach braced
  3. Sweep the ball across your body from one hip toward the opposite shoulder
  4. Let your feet pivot slightly but keep the squat depth constant
  5. Control it back across and repeat, then work the other direction
ea_low_rotational_med_ball_chops_quarter_squat_rotating_med_ball_left_and_ride_across_core anklehipknee

Low Sled Push

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposePushing from the low handles puts you in a more horizontal position, which shifts the work further onto the legs and makes it closer to a sprint start. Brutal on the quadriceps and completely safe.

  1. Load the sled and grip the low handles with straight arms
  2. Get your body as close to horizontal as you can while keeping your back flat
  3. Set your feet behind you and brace your stomach
  4. Drive forward with short, hard steps through the balls of your feet
  5. Push for the set distance, then rest fully before the next effort
ea_low_sled_push

Lying Neck Curls

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeStrengthens the front of the neck, which matters for anyone in a contact sport and for anyone whose head sits forward from screen use. Start with no weight at all and add it very slowly.

  1. Lie face up on a bench with your head and neck extending past the end
  2. Support your head at first, or place a folded towel under it
  3. Let your head lower back slowly until you feel a gentle stretch
