  3. Keep your chest up, your heels down and your knees over your toes
  4. Hold that position for the set time, breathing normally
  5. Stand up under control rather than collapsing out of the hold
ea_plate_squat_hold anklehipknee

Plate Squat Hold Biceps Curl

Legs

PurposeCurling while holding the bottom of a squat keeps the legs under constant tension while the arms work, so a single plate covers two jobs. Efficient, and it makes the squat hold considerably harder to keep clean.

  1. Hold a plate at your chest and squat down to about parallel
  2. Hold that depth with your chest up and heels planted
  3. Extend your arms to lower the plate down in front of you
  4. Curl it back to your chest without letting your torso tip forward
  5. Continue curling for the set, then stand up out of the hold
ea_plate_squat_hold_biceps_curl anklehipknee

Plate Squat Hold Reach

Legs

PurposeReaching forward from the bottom of a squat pulls your balance toward your toes, so the legs and the stomach have to work harder to hold the position. A simple way to make a squat hold much more demanding without more weight.

  1. Hold a plate at your chest and squat down to about parallel
  2. Keep your heels flat and your chest tall in the hold
  3. Push the plate straight out in front of you until the arms are extended
  4. Hold it there without letting your heels lift or your back round
  5. Draw it back to your chest and repeat for the set
ea_plate_squat_hold_reach anklehipknee

Plate Squat Reach

Legs

PurposeAdds an arm reach to each squat, so every repetition includes a moment where the load moves away from your body and your trunk has to hold it. It turns a plain squat into a whole-body exercise.

  1. Hold a plate at your chest with both hands and stand with feet shoulder width
  2. Squat down until your thighs are about parallel with the floor
  3. At the bottom, push the plate straight out in front of you
  4. Bring it back to your chest before you start standing
  5. Stand up fully and repeat for the set
ea_plate_squat_reach anklehipknee

Plate Staggered Deadlift

Legs

PurposeMost of the weight goes through the front leg while the back foot only steadies you, so each side gets trained without needing single-leg balance. The practical way to even out a stronger and weaker leg.

  1. Stand with one foot forward and the other half a step back with the heel raised
  2. Hold a plate with both hands in front of your thighs
  3. Put about eighty percent of your weight on the front foot
  4. Hinge at the hips and lower the plate along the front leg with a flat back
  5. Drive through the front heel to stand, then swap the stance
ea_plate_staggered_deadlift hiplower_back

Plate Staggered Pinch Grip Deadlift

Legs

PurposeThe staggered stance loads one leg while the pinch grip loads the fingers, so this trains the hinge and the grip in the same set. Grip usually fails first, which makes it a natural way to cap the load.

  1. Stand with one foot forward and the other half a step back, heel raised
  2. Pinch a plate in each hand by the smooth outer face, arms hanging
  3. Shift most of your weight onto the front foot
  4. Hinge at the hips and lower the plates along the front leg, back flat
  5. Stand back up through the front heel, then change the stance
ea_plate_staggered_pinch_grip_deadlift hiplower_back

Sissy Squat Bodyweight

Legs

PurposeLoads the front of the thigh through a stretch almost nothing else reaches, by letting the knees travel far forward while the hips stay open. Build up slowly — the knees need time to adapt to this position.

  1. Hold a bench or rail with one hand and stand tall with feet hip width
  2. Rise onto the balls of your feet and keep your hips pushed forward
  3. Let your knees travel forward as you lean your torso back in a straight line
  4. Lower as far as you can control, keeping hips, chest and head aligned
  5. Pull yourself back up using the front of the thighs, not by bending at the hips
ea_sissy_squat_bodyweight anklehipknee

Smith Machine Narrow Stance Heels Elevated Squats

Legs

PurposeNarrow feet and raised heels point the work at the front of the thigh, and the fixed bar path lets you stay in that upright position without fighting for balance. The most direct quadriceps squat available.

  1. Place a small plate or wedge under your heels and stand under the bar
  2. Set your feet close together, slightly in front of the bar, and unlock it
  3. Keep your chest tall and your torso as upright as the machine allows
  4. Squat straight down as deep as you can control, knees travelling forward
  5. Drive back up without letting your heels leave the wedge
ea_smith_machine_narrow_stance_heels_elevated_squats anklehipknee

Standing Cable Hip Flexion

Legs

PurposeTrains the muscles that lift the knee, which running and sprinting depend on and which almost no gym exercise loads directly. Weakness there shows up as a stride that shortens when you get tired.

  1. Attach an ankle strap to a low pulley and fasten it around one ankle
  2. Stand facing away from the machine and hold something stable for balance
  3. Stand tall on the other leg with the working leg slightly behind you
  4. Drive the knee up and forward against the cable until the thigh is about parallel to the floor
  5. Lower slowly back past the standing leg, then switch sides
ea_standing_cable_hip_flexion

Barbell Hang Clean

Powerlifting

PurposeTeaches the body to produce force fast rather than merely to lift a lot. Starting from the hang removes the floor pull, so the whole exercise is the hip snap — the same explosive extension behind a jump, a sprint start and a throw.

  1. Stand holding the bar at arm's length, hands just outside the hips, feet hip-width
  2. Push the hips back and slide the bar down the thighs to just above the knee, back flat, chest up
  3. Drive the hips forward hard and shrug — the bar is thrown upward by the legs, not pulled by the arms
  4. As it rises, drop under it and spin the elbows through to catch the bar on the front of the shoulders
  5. Stand up out of the catch, then lower the bar back to the hang and reset before the next rep
ea_barbell_hang_clean lower_backwrist

Barbell Press Under

Powerlifting

PurposeDrills the second half of a clean or snatch — the moment you stop pushing the bar up and start pushing yourself down under it. Most missed lifts are not a weak pull, they are a slow turnover, and this is how that gets faster.

  1. Hold the bar at the front of the shoulders with a light load — this is a technique drill, not a strength lift
  2. Keep the bar path vertical and the torso upright throughout
  3. Press yourself DOWN under the bar rather than pressing the bar up, dropping into a quarter squat
  4. Lock the arms overhead at the same moment your hips stop descending
  5. Stand up under control and reset; add weight only once the two happen together
ea_barbell_press_under kneeshoulder

Plate Clean

Powerlifting

PurposeThe hip drive of a barbell clean with none of its technical cost. A plate is easier to hold, easier to bail, and lets you rehearse the explosive extension long before a loaded bar is a sensible idea.

  1. Stand with the plate on the floor between your feet, held at its sides with both hands
  2. Hinge at the hips with a flat back and grip the plate low
  3. Drive through the floor and extend the hips hard, letting the plate float upward
  4. Pull yourself under it and catch it at chest height with the elbows up
  5. Lower it back to the floor under control rather than dropping it
ea_plate_clean lower_backwrist

Plate Clean and Press

Powerlifting

PurposeOne movement from the floor to overhead, so legs, trunk and shoulders have to hand the load off to each other without a pause. That handover is what makes it a conditioning exercise as much as a strength one.

  1. Start with the plate on the floor between your feet, gripped at the sides
  2. Hinge, then extend the hips explosively and catch the plate at chest height
  3. Without resetting, brace the trunk and press the plate straight overhead
  4. Keep the ribs down — the lower back should not arch to finish the press
  5. Return the plate to the chest, then to the floor, and repeat
ea_plate_clean_and_press kneelower_backshoulderwrist

Plate Thruster

Powerlifting

PurposeA front squat and an overhead press joined into one rep, which is why it raises the heart rate faster than either alone. The legs finish the squat and the arms start the press at the same instant — that overlap is the whole point.

  1. Hold the plate at chest height with both hands, feet shoulder-width
  2. Squat down as deep as you can while keeping the chest tall and the heels down
  3. Stand up out of the squat and, without pausing, use that momentum to press the plate overhead
  4. Lock the arms out fully with the plate over the middle of your feet
  5. Bring it back to the chest as you descend into the next rep
ea_plate_thruster

Sandbag Cleans

Powerlifting

PurposeA clean with a load that shifts while you lift it. The sand moves, so the trunk has to correct continuously — closer to carrying a person or a piece of furniture than any barbell lift will ever be.

  1. Stand over the bag with feet hip-width and grip it by the handles or hug it at the sides
  2. Hinge at the hips, keep the back flat, and pull the bag to the top of the thighs
  3. Extend the hips hard and pull the bag up the body, keeping it in contact
  4. Drop the elbows under and catch it high on the chest, hugging it tight
  5. Lower it to the floor under control — resist the urge to let it drop and yank your back
ea_sandbag_cleans lower_backwrist

Cable 30 Degree Shrug

Shoulders

PurposeA shrug angled forward instead of straight up, which puts the work into the part of the trapezius that runs down between the shoulder blades rather than the part that already gets used all day. That lower section is what holds the shoulder blades in place.

  1. Set two low handles and stand facing the machine holding one in each hand
  2. Step back and lean your torso forward about thirty degrees, back flat
  3. Let the cables pull your shoulders forward and down at the start
  4. Shrug your shoulder blades back and down along the line of your torso, arms straight
  5. Hold the squeeze briefly, then let the blades travel forward again under control
ea_cable_30_degree_shrug lower_backneckupper_back

Cable Face Pull with Rope

Shoulders

PurposeOne of the few exercises that trains the small muscles at the back of the shoulder, which get outnumbered by everything that presses. Doing these regularly is what keeps a heavy bench-press habit from slowly closing your shoulders forward.

  1. Attach a rope to a pulley set at about head height and step back until the cable is tight
  2. Hold one end in each hand with your thumbs pointing back
  3. Pull the rope toward your face, splitting your hands apart as it comes
  4. Finish with your hands beside your ears and your elbows level with your shoulders
  5. Return slowly, letting the shoulder blades reach forward at the end
ea_cable_face_pull_with_rope shoulderupper_back

Cable Single Arm Reverse Fly

Shoulders

PurposeWorks the rear shoulder one side at a time against constant cable tension, so it keeps pulling at the end of the range where a dumbbell version has nothing left. That end position is where the rear shoulder actually needs the work.

  1. Set a handle at chest height and stand side-on, taking it with the far hand across your body
  2. Step out until the cable is tight, arm straight in front of your chest
  3. Keep a small fixed bend in the elbow and brace your stomach
  4. Sweep the arm out and back in a wide arc until it is in line with your shoulder
  5. Return slowly across the body without turning your torso, then swap sides
ea_cable_single_arm_reverse_fly shoulderupper_back

Dumbbell Alternating Arnold Press

Shoulders

PurposeThe rotation on the way up takes the shoulder through its full range, so the front and side of the muscle both get worked in one press. Alternating arms means the shoulder that is not pressing gets a moment to recover, which lets you keep the form clean for longer.

  1. Sit or stand holding two dumbbells at chest height, palms facing you
  2. Press one dumbbell up while rotating the palm to face forward
  3. Finish overhead with the arm straight and the palm forward
  4. Reverse the path exactly — rotate back as you lower to the chest
  5. Repeat with the other arm, alternating for the whole set
ea_dumbbell_alternating_arnold_press shoulder

Dumbbell Chest Supported Y Raise

Shoulders

PurposeLying face down takes the lower back out of it entirely, so the small muscles between and below the shoulder blades have to lift the weight themselves. Raising the arms in a Y is the shape that reaches the lower trapezius, which almost nothing else does.

  1. Set a bench to a low incline and lie face down with your chest on the pad
  2. Hold a light dumbbell in each hand, arms hanging straight down, thumbs up
  3. Keep your neck long and your chin gently tucked
  4. Raise both arms up and out to form a Y with your body, thumbs leading
  5. Stop at shoulder height or a little above, then lower slowly
ea_dumbbell_chest_supported_y_raise shoulder

Dumbbell Laying 30 Degree Shrug

Shoulders

PurposeLying on an incline changes the direction of the load, so the shrug pulls the shoulder blades down and back instead of straight up. That is the direction that helps posture rather than the one that builds a thicker neck.

  1. Set a bench to about thirty degrees and lie face down on it, chest supported
  2. Hold a dumbbell in each hand with the arms hanging straight down
  3. Let your shoulder blades slide forward and apart at the start
  4. Draw the blades back and down toward your hips, arms staying straight
  5. Hold the position for a second, then lower under control
ea_dumbbell_laying_30_degree_shrug lower_backneckupper_back

Dumbbell Laying Silverback Shrug

Shoulders

PurposeA face-down shrug that targets the middle of the trapezius — the section between the shoulder blades that holds them against the ribs. Weak there is why shoulders drift forward and why heavy pulling feels unstable.

  1. Lie face down on an incline bench with a dumbbell in each hand
  2. Let the arms hang straight down and allow the shoulder blades to spread apart
  3. Keep the elbows locked straight for the whole movement
  4. Squeeze the shoulder blades toward each other without bending the arms
  5. Pause at the fully squeezed position, then release slowly
ea_dumbbell_laying_silverback_shrug lower_backneckupper_back

Dumbbell Plank Pullthrough

Shoulders

PurposeReaching under your body to drag a weight while holding a plank forces the shoulder that stays down to hold the whole load, and the stomach to stop the hips rotating. Two jobs at once, and neither can be faked.

  1. Set up in a high plank with a dumbbell on the floor just outside one hand
  2. Widen your feet for balance and squeeze your glutes and stomach
  3. Reach under your chest with the opposite hand and grip the dumbbell
  4. Drag it across to the other side while keeping your hips completely level
  5. Return that hand to the floor and repeat, alternating sides
ea_dumbbell_plank_pullthrough elbowwrist

Dumbbell Shoulder Extension

Shoulders

PurposeTaking the arms behind the body works the back of the shoulder and the lats through a range that almost nothing else uses. It directly opens the front of the shoulders, which is where the tightness from sitting collects.

  1. Stand tall with a light dumbbell in each hand, arms by your sides, palms facing back
  2. Keep the ribs down and the chest open, without arching the lower back
  3. Sweep both arms straight back behind you with the elbows locked
  4. Go only as far as the shoulders allow without the chest collapsing forward
  5. Return to your sides slowly, resisting the weight the whole way
ea_dumbbell_shoulder_extension

Dumbbell Silverback Shrug

Shoulders

PurposeA bent-over shrug with no bench, so your back has to hold the position while the middle trapezius does the work. Harder on the lower back than the supported version, and better for learning to hold a hinge.

  1. Stand with feet hip width and a dumbbell in each hand
  2. Hinge forward from the hips with a flat back until your torso is at about forty-five degrees
  3. Let the arms hang straight and the shoulder blades spread apart
  4. Squeeze the blades together and slightly down without bending the elbows
  5. Hold for a second, then let them spread again under control
ea_dumbbell_silverback_shrug lower_backneckupper_back

Dumbbell Single Arm Upright Row

Shoulders

PurposeBuilds the side of the shoulder and the upper trapezius together. Using one arm lets the elbow travel on the path your own shoulder prefers, which is what makes this safer than the two-handed barbell version many people find pinching.

  1. Stand tall with a dumbbell in one hand resting against the front of your thigh
  2. Put the other hand on your hip and keep your shoulders level
  3. Pull the dumbbell straight up close to your body, leading with the elbow
  4. Stop when the elbow reaches shoulder height — no higher
  5. Lower slowly to the thigh, then finish the set and change arms
ea_dumbbell_single_arm_upright_row neckshoulderupper_back

Elevated Pike Shoulder Shrug

Shoulders

PurposeWith your feet raised and hips high, your own bodyweight loads the shoulders — the closest most people get to overhead pressing without a weight. It also trains the shoulder blades to move properly under load, which matters before any handstand work.

  1. Place your feet on a box and walk your hands back until your hips are stacked high over your shoulders
  2. Keep your arms straight and your head between your upper arms
  3. Let your shoulder blades rise up toward your ears without bending the elbows
  4. Push the floor away and press your shoulders down away from your ears
  5. Move slowly between the two positions, keeping the hips high throughout
ea_elevated_pike_shoulder_shrug lower_backneckshoulderupper_back

Kettlebell Front Raise

Shoulders

PurposeIsolates the front of the shoulder, the part that lifts things in front of you. The bell hangs below the hand, so the wrist has to stay strong the whole way — the load pulls it back if you let it.

  1. Stand tall holding a kettlebell in front of one thigh, or one in each hand
  2. Brace your stomach and keep your ribs down so you cannot lean back
  3. Raise the arm straight out in front of you with only a slight bend in the elbow
  4. Stop at shoulder height with the wrist straight and the bell steady
  5. Lower slowly to the thigh without letting the weight swing
ea_kettlebell_front_raise shoulder

Kettlebell Incline Shrug

Shoulders

PurposeThe incline angle lets the shoulder blades move down as well as back, which is the direction that supports the shoulder joint. Straight-up shrugs only train one of those and are far more common than they need to be.

  1. Lie face down on an incline bench with a kettlebell in each hand
  2. Let the arms hang and the shoulder blades spread apart at the bottom
  3. Keep the elbows straight and the neck relaxed
  4. Pull the shoulder blades back and down along the angle of the bench
  5. Hold briefly at the top, then lower under control
ea_kettlebell_incline_shrug lower_backneckupper_back

Kettlebell Long Lever Lateral Raise

Shoulders

PurposeHolding the bell further from the body makes a light weight feel heavy, so the side of the shoulder gets a hard set without loading the joint. Useful when you want intensity but the shoulder cannot take a heavy dumbbell.

  1. Stand tall with a light kettlebell in one hand, arm hanging by your side
  2. Straighten the arm fully and keep it straight for the whole set
  3. Raise the arm out to the side in a wide arc, keeping the bell far from your body
  4. Stop at shoulder height, with the shoulder staying down away from the ear
  5. Lower slowly along the same wide path, then switch sides
ea_kettlebell_long_lever_lateral_raise shoulder

Kettlebell Rear Delt Row

Shoulders

PurposeA row with the elbows flared wide, which pulls the work off the lats and onto the rear shoulders and upper back. Those are the muscles that balance out a chest-heavy training week.

  1. Hinge forward from the hips with a flat back, a kettlebell in each hand
  2. Let the arms hang straight down under your shoulders
  3. Row both bells upward with the elbows travelling out wide, away from your body
  4. Finish with the upper arms in line with your shoulders and the blades squeezed
  5. Lower slowly to the hanging position without rounding the back
ea_kettlebell_rear_delt_row shoulderupper_back

Kettlebell Shoulder Extension

Shoulders

PurposeDrives the arms back behind the body, which opens the chest and works the back of the shoulder in the range that sitting takes away. A small movement with an outsized effect on how upright you stand.

  1. Stand tall with a kettlebell in each hand, arms at your sides, palms facing back
  2. Set your ribs down and squeeze your glutes so the lower back stays neutral
  3. Sweep both straight arms backwards behind your hips
  4. Stop where the chest starts to want to collapse forward
  5. Return slowly to your sides, keeping the shoulders down throughout
ea_kettlebell_shoulder_extension

Kettlebell Shrug

Shoulders

PurposeThe straightforward way to build the upper trapezius, the muscle that carries any load hanging from your hands. Kettlebells sit closer to the body than dumbbells, so heavy sets stay easier to control.

  1. Stand tall with a kettlebell hanging in each hand at your sides
  2. Keep your arms straight and your chin level
  3. Lift your shoulders straight up toward your ears as high as they will go
  4. Hold the top for a second without rolling the shoulders
  5. Lower slowly and let the shoulders settle fully before the next repetition
ea_kettlebell_shrug lower_backneckupper_back

Kettlebell Silverback Shrug

Shoulders

PurposeBent forward, the shrug pulls the blades together rather than up, so it builds the middle back that holds your posture. This is the version to do if your upper traps are already tight from stress or desk work.

  1. Hinge forward at the hips with a flat back, a kettlebell in each hand
  2. Let the arms hang straight and the shoulder blades spread wide
  3. Keep the elbows completely straight throughout
  4. Draw the shoulder blades together and slightly down
  5. Pause at the squeeze, then let them spread apart again slowly
ea_kettlebell_silverback_shrug lower_backneckupper_back

Kettlebell Single Arm Lateral Raise

Shoulders

PurposeBuilds the side of the shoulder, which is what makes shoulders look wide. One arm at a time lets you hold something with the other hand for balance, so the body cannot swing the weight up.

  1. Stand tall with a kettlebell in one hand, the other hand on a rack or your hip
  2. Let the bell hang beside your thigh with a slight bend in the elbow
  3. Raise the arm out to the side, leading with the elbow rather than the hand
  4. Stop at shoulder height, keeping the shoulder pressed down away from your ear
  5. Lower slowly, then finish the set and change arms
ea_kettlebell_single_arm_lateral_raise shoulder

Kettlebell Single Arm Rear Delt Fly

Shoulders

PurposeWorks the back of one shoulder while the stomach stops the torso from twisting toward the weight. That anti-twist job is what a two-arm fly never trains, and it is why this feels harder than the weight suggests.

  1. Hinge forward with a flat back, one hand braced on a bench for support
  2. Hold a light kettlebell in the free hand, hanging straight down
  3. Keep a small fixed bend in the working elbow
  4. Raise the arm out to the side until it is level with your shoulder, without rotating your torso
  5. Lower slowly to the hanging position, then switch sides
ea_kettlebell_single_arm_rear_delt_fly shoulderupper_back

Kettlebell Upright Row

Shoulders

PurposeTrains the side of the shoulder and the upper trapezius together in one pull. Keep the elbows below shoulder height — going higher is what turns this exercise into shoulder pain for a lot of people.

  1. Stand tall with a kettlebell in each hand, resting against the front of your thighs
  2. Keep your back straight and your stomach braced
  3. Pull both bells straight up the front of your body, leading with the elbows
  4. Stop when the elbows reach shoulder height, no higher
  5. Lower under control to the thighs and reset before the next repetition
ea_kettlebell_upright_row neckshoulderupper_back

Landmine Alternating Single Arm Press

Shoulders

PurposeThe landmine presses on an arc rather than straight overhead, which most shoulders tolerate far better than a vertical press. Alternating arms means your stomach has to resist being pulled sideways with every repetition.

  1. Stand facing away from the landmine with the loaded bar end at one shoulder
  2. Hold the end in that hand, feet shoulder width apart, stomach braced
  3. Press the bar up and forward until the arm is straight, following its arc
  4. Bring it back to the shoulder and pass the end to the other hand
  5. Press with that arm the same way, alternating for the whole set
ea_landmine_alternating_single_arm_press shoulder

Landmine Half Kneeling Single Arm Overhead Press

Shoulders

PurposeHalf kneeling locks the hips, so you cannot lean back and turn the press into a throw. It exposes exactly how much of your overhead strength comes from the shoulder and how much came from your lower back.

  1. Kneel on one knee facing away from the landmine, the down knee under your hip
  2. Hold the loaded bar end in the hand on the same side as the down knee
  3. Squeeze the glute of the kneeling leg and pull your ribs down
  4. Press the bar up and forward until the arm is straight, back staying upright
  5. Lower to the shoulder under control, then finish the set and switch sides
ea_landmine_half_kneeling_single_arm_overhead_press kneeshoulder

Landmine Kneeling Alternating Overhead Press

Shoulders

PurposeKneeling on both knees removes the legs entirely, so the shoulders press without any help. Alternating keeps one arm loaded at all times, which keeps the stomach working right through the set.

  1. Kneel on both knees facing away from the landmine, hips upright over the knees
  2. Take the loaded bar end in one hand at shoulder height
  3. Squeeze your glutes and keep your ribs pulled down
  4. Press the bar out and up until the arm is straight, then return to the shoulder
  5. Pass the end to the other hand and repeat, alternating throughout
ea_landmine_kneeling_alternating_overhead_press kneeshoulder

Landmine Kneeling Overhead Press

Shoulders

PurposeA pressing position that gives the shoulder the arc it likes while the kneeling stance stops the lower back from arching to help. Good for anyone whose overhead press turns into a leaning-back contest.

  1. Kneel on both knees facing away from the landmine with your hips tall
  2. Cup the loaded end of the bar with both hands at chest height
  3. Brace your stomach and squeeze your glutes to lock the hips
  4. Press the bar up and forward along its arc until your arms are straight
  5. Lower it back to your chest slowly without letting your back arch
ea_landmine_kneeling_overhead_press kneeshoulder

Landmine Lateral Raise

Shoulders

PurposeThe landmine's arc changes the resistance as the arm rises, so the hardest point lands nearer the top than with a dumbbell. That is where the side of the shoulder is normally weakest and least trained.

  1. Stand side-on to the landmine and hold the loaded end in the outside hand
  2. Let the arm hang across the front of your body with a slight elbow bend
  3. Set your feet shoulder width and brace your stomach
  4. Raise the arm out to the side along the bar's arc, to about shoulder height
  5. Lower slowly along the same path, then move round and change sides
ea_landmine_lateral_raise shoulder

Landmine Overhead Press

Shoulders

PurposeThe standing landmine press builds real overhead strength on a path the shoulder finds comfortable, and lets the legs contribute a little. Often the heaviest pressing available to someone who cannot go straight overhead without pain.

  1. Stand facing away from the landmine and cup the loaded bar end with both hands at your chest
  2. Set your feet shoulder width apart with a slight bend in the knees
  3. Brace your stomach and pull the ribs down
  4. Press the bar up and forward until your arms lock out
  5. Lower it under control to your chest and reset before the next repetition
ea_landmine_overhead_press shoulder

Landmine Seated Alternating Overhead Press

Shoulders

PurposeSitting takes the legs out completely and the alternating rhythm keeps one side under load at all times. It is the strictest way to press with a landmine, and the honest test of shoulder strength alone.

  1. Sit on a bench or the floor facing away from the landmine, back upright
  2. Take the loaded bar end in one hand at shoulder height
  3. Brace your stomach so your torso does not lean or twist
  4. Press up and forward to a straight arm, then bring it back to the shoulder
  5. Hand the bar to the other side and repeat, alternating for the whole set
ea_landmine_seated_alternating_overhead_press shoulder

Landmine Seated Overhead Press

Shoulders

PurposeSeated pressing removes any leg drive, so every kilo comes from the shoulders and upper back. With the landmine's arc it stays comfortable for shoulders that do not like a barbell overhead.

  1. Sit facing away from the landmine with your back tall and feet planted
  2. Cup the loaded end of the bar with both hands at chest height
  3. Take a breath and lock your stomach before pressing
  4. Push the bar up and forward until your arms are straight
  5. Lower slowly to your chest, keeping your back from arching
ea_landmine_seated_overhead_press shoulder

Landmine Seated Single Arm Overhead Press

Shoulders

PurposeOne arm, seated, so nothing can help: not the legs, not the other side, not a lean. It shows a side-to-side strength difference more clearly than any two-handed press, and lets you fix it.

  1. Sit facing away from the landmine with your feet flat and your back tall
  2. Hold the loaded bar end in one hand at shoulder height
  3. Rest the free hand on your thigh and keep your shoulders level
  4. Press up and forward until the arm is straight, without leaning away
  5. Lower under control, complete the set, then match the reps on the other side
ea_landmine_seated_single_arm_overhead_press shoulder

Landmine Single Arm Push Press

Shoulders

PurposeA short dip and drive from the legs lets you move more weight than the shoulder could press on its own, which trains power rather than just strength. Useful once a strict press is already solid.

  1. Stand facing away from the landmine holding the loaded end at one shoulder
  2. Dip by bending the knees a few centimetres, keeping your torso upright
  3. Drive up hard through the legs and let that momentum start the bar moving
  4. Finish the press with the arm, locking it straight out along the bar's arc
  5. Lower the bar to the shoulder under control and reset before the next rep
ea_landmine_single_arm_push_press shoulder

Landmine Single Arm Staggered Overhead Press

Shoulders

PurposeThe staggered stance narrows your base, so the stomach and hips have to work to keep you square while one arm presses. A step between a two-footed press and a kneeling one.

  1. Stand facing away from the landmine and step one foot forward into a short stagger
  2. Hold the loaded end at the shoulder of the arm on the same side as the back foot
  3. Square your hips and shoulders and brace your stomach
  4. Press the bar up and forward until the arm is straight, staying square throughout
  5. Lower to the shoulder, finish the set, then swap the stance and the arm
ea_landmine_single_arm_staggered_overhead_press shoulder

Laying Lateral Raise

Shoulders

PurposeLying on your side changes where the load is heaviest: the bottom of the movement becomes the hard part, instead of the top. That reaches the side of the shoulder in a range a standing raise leaves almost unloaded.

  1. Lie on your side on a bench or the floor with the top arm resting along your body
  2. Hold a light dumbbell in the top hand with a slight bend in the elbow
  3. Support your head with the bottom arm and keep your body in a straight line
  4. Raise the dumbbell up toward the ceiling until the arm is vertical
  5. Lower slowly back to your body, then roll over and do the other side
ea_laying_lateral_raise shoulder

Plate Car Driver

Shoulders

PurposeRotating a plate held out in front of you trains the front of the shoulders to hold a position while the forearms turn under load. It looks easy and stops being easy after about twenty seconds.

  1. Hold a plate like a steering wheel with both hands at chest height
  2. Extend your arms straight out in front of you at shoulder level
  3. Brace your stomach and keep the ribs down so you cannot lean back
  4. Rotate the plate to one side as if turning a wheel, keeping the arms straight
  5. Rotate to the other side and continue back and forth for the set
ea_plate_car_driver

Plate Full Front Raise

Shoulders

PurposeTaking the plate from the hips all the way overhead trains the front of the shoulder through its whole range in one movement, rather than stopping at shoulder height like most front raises do.

  1. Hold a plate at the sides with both hands, arms hanging in front of your thighs
  2. Stand tall with your stomach braced and ribs pulled down
  3. Raise the plate with straight arms up to shoulder height
  4. Continue lifting it overhead until your arms are beside your ears
  5. Lower slowly all the way back to your thighs without swinging
ea_plate_full_front_raise shoulder

Plate Halo

Shoulders

PurposeCircling a plate around your head takes the shoulders through their full range under a light load, which is why it works as both a warm-up and a mobility drill. It is the standard opener before overhead work.

  1. Hold a light plate with both hands in front of your chest
  2. Stand tall with your stomach braced and your ribs down
  3. Circle the plate around your head, passing it close behind the neck
  4. Keep the movement slow and let the elbows travel rather than the torso
  5. Complete the circles in one direction, then do the same number the other way
ea_plate_halo

Plate Internally Rotated Rear Delt Fly

Shoulders

PurposeTurning the thumbs down aims the work squarely at the rear shoulder and takes the middle back out of it. Use light plates — this position is unforgiving of weight, and the point is placement, not load.

  1. Hinge forward with a flat back, holding a light plate in each hand
  2. Let the arms hang straight down and rotate them so the thumbs point toward the floor
  3. Keep a small fixed bend in the elbows
  4. Raise both arms out to the sides until level with your shoulders
  5. Lower slowly, keeping the thumbs pointing down the whole time
ea_plate_internally_rotated_rear_delt_fly shoulderupper_back

Plate Lateral Raise

Shoulders

PurposeHolding a plate rather than a dumbbell puts the weight further from your hand, so a light plate loads the side of the shoulder as hard as a heavier dumbbell would. Kinder on the joint for the same effect.

  1. Hold a plate in each hand by the rim, arms hanging at your sides
  2. Stand tall with a slight bend in the elbows and your shoulders down
  3. Raise both plates out to the sides in a wide arc
  4. Stop at shoulder height without shrugging the shoulders up
  5. Lower slowly along the same path, resisting the weight all the way down
ea_plate_lateral_raise shoulder

Plate Overhead Press to Tricep Extension

Shoulders

PurposeChains a shoulder press into a triceps extension without setting the weight down, so the whole back of the arm and the shoulder get worked in one continuous set. Efficient when you have one plate and little time.

  1. Hold a plate at the sides with both hands at chest height
  2. Press it straight overhead until your arms lock out
  3. Keeping the upper arms still, bend the elbows to lower the plate behind your head
  4. Extend the elbows to push it back overhead
  5. Lower the plate to your chest — that is one full repetition
ea_plate_overhead_press_to_tricep_extension elbowshoulder

Plate Overhead Shrug

Shoulders

PurposeShrugging with the arms overhead trains the lower trapezius, the part that pulls the shoulder blades down. Strength there is what makes overhead pressing feel stable instead of pinched.

  1. Press a plate overhead with both hands and lock your arms straight
  2. Let your shoulders rise toward your ears while keeping the elbows locked
  3. Brace your stomach so your lower back does not arch
  4. Push the plate higher by pressing your shoulders up and away from your ears
  5. Return to the starting position slowly, keeping the arms straight throughout
ea_plate_overhead_shrug lower_backneckshoulderupper_back

Plate Reach

Shoulders

PurposeHolding a plate out at arm's length is a test of how long the front of your shoulders can hold a position, which is a different quality from how much they can lift. It also makes the stomach work to stop you leaning back.

  1. Hold a plate with both hands against your chest, standing tall
  2. Brace your stomach and pull your ribs down
  3. Push the plate straight out in front of you until the arms are fully extended
  4. Hold it there at shoulder height for the prescribed time
  5. Draw it back to your chest under control without letting it drop
ea_plate_reach

Plate Rear Delt Fly

Shoulders

PurposeWorks the back of the shoulders, the muscles that pull the shoulders back and undo the forward rounding that comes with pressing and desk work. Light weight and a full squeeze matter far more than load here.

  1. Hinge forward from the hips with a flat back, a light plate in each hand
  2. Let the arms hang straight down beneath your shoulders
  3. Keep a small fixed bend in the elbows for the whole set
  4. Raise both plates out to the sides until they are level with your shoulders
  5. Squeeze for a second, then lower slowly under control
ea_plate_rear_delt_fly shoulderupper_back

Seated Dumbbell Neutral Grip Front Raises

Shoulders

PurposeSitting stops you from swinging the weight up with your hips, and the neutral grip is easier on the front of the shoulder than turning the palms down. The strictest way to train the front delts.

  1. Sit on the end of a bench with a dumbbell in each hand, palms facing each other
  2. Sit tall with your feet flat and your back straight
  3. Raise both dumbbells straight out in front of you, thumbs pointing up
  4. Stop at shoulder height without leaning back
  5. Lower slowly to your thighs, keeping the palms facing each other throughout
ea_seated_dumbbell_neutral_grip_front_raises shoulder

Seated Dumbbell Neutral Grip Side Raises

Shoulders

PurposeSeated raises remove every trace of leg drive, so the side of the shoulder does all of the work with a weight far lighter than you would use standing. That is the point — this muscle responds to precision, not to load.

  1. Sit upright on the end of a bench with a dumbbell in each hand at your sides
  2. Keep the palms facing each other and a slight bend in the elbows
  3. Raise both arms out to the sides in a wide arc
  4. Stop at shoulder height with the shoulders staying down, not shrugged
  5. Lower slowly to your sides without letting the weights drop
ea_seated_dumbbell_neutral_grip_side_raises shoulder

Suspension Trainer with Grips Inverted Row on Floor

Shoulders

PurposeA pull where your own body is the weight and your feet set the difficulty, so it scales from very easy to very hard without changing equipment. It builds the upper back and rear shoulders that balance out pressing.

  1. Set the straps so the handles hang at about hip height and take one in each hand
  2. Walk your feet forward and lean back until your arms are straight
  3. Squeeze your glutes and stomach so your body forms a straight line
  4. Pull your chest up to the handles, drawing your elbows past your ribs
  5. Lower yourself slowly to straight arms without letting the hips sag
ea_suspension_trainer_with_grips_inverted_row_on_floor upper_back

Arms Behind Back Chest Stretch

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeOpens the front of the chest and the shoulders, which shorten from hours of sitting with the arms in front of you. Doing it between sets of pressing keeps the shoulders from closing up during the session.

  1. Stand tall and clasp your hands together behind your back
  2. Straighten your arms and roll your shoulders back and down
  3. Lift your hands away from your body until you feel the chest open
  4. Keep your ribs down — do not arch your lower back to go further
  5. Breathe slowly and hold for twenty to thirty seconds
ea_arms_behind_back_chest_stretch

Arms Wide Chest Stretch

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeStretches the chest with the arms out to the sides, which reaches the fibres a behind-the-back stretch misses. Useful before pressing, when the chest needs to be long rather than short and tight.

  1. Stand tall with your feet hip width apart
  2. Open both arms out wide to the sides at shoulder height, palms forward
  3. Draw your shoulder blades together and press your chest forward
  4. Keep your chin level and your ribs pulled down
  5. Hold for twenty to thirty seconds, breathing into the chest
ea_arms_wide_chest_stretch

Both Arms Behind on Wall Biceps Stretch

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeStretches the biceps and the front of both shoulders at once, which is where tightness collects after pulling work or a day at a keyboard. The wall does the work, so you can relax into it.

  1. Stand with your back to a wall, about half a step away
  2. Place both palms flat on the wall behind you at hip height, fingers pointing down
  3. Keep your arms straight and your chest lifted
  4. Slowly bend your knees to lower your body until you feel the stretch through the biceps
  5. Hold for twenty to thirty seconds without letting the shoulders shrug up
ea_both_arms_behind_on_wall_biceps_stretch

Bulgarian Split Squat Stretch

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeStretches the front of the back hip, which shortens in anyone who sits for a living and which limits how upright you can stand under a bar. This is the position that opens it.

  1. Place the top of one foot on a bench behind you and step the other foot forward
  2. Lower your back knee toward the floor with your torso upright
  3. Squeeze the glute of the back leg to push the hip forward
  4. Stop where you feel a stretch across the front of the back thigh, not in the knee
  5. Hold for twenty to thirty seconds, then change legs
ea_bulgarian_split_squat_stretch anklehipknee

Calf Push Stretch with Hands Against Wall V.2

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeStretches the large calf muscle with the knee straight, which is the one that limits ankle movement and, through it, squat depth. Tight calves are a very common reason heels lift in a squat.

  1. Stand facing a wall and place both hands on it at shoulder height
  2. Step one foot well back, keeping that leg completely straight
  3. Press the back heel firmly into the floor with the toes pointing forward
  4. Lean your hips toward the wall until you feel the calf stretch
  5. Hold for thirty seconds, then swap legs
ea_calf_push_stretch_with_hands_against_wall_v_2 ankle

Calve Stretch Foot on Wall

Stretching - Mobility

PurposePutting the toes up the wall stretches the calf and the tissue under the foot at the same time, which is the combination that helps with heel pain from plantar fasciitis.

  1. Stand facing a wall and place the ball of one foot against it, heel on the floor
  2. Keep that leg straight and your toes pointing up the wall
  3. Place your hands on the wall for support
  4. Gently lean your hips and chest toward the wall until the calf stretches
  5. Hold for thirty seconds, then change feet
ea_calve_stretch_foot_on_wall

Calve Stretch From Wall to Floor

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeMoves the stretch along the whole calf as the angle changes, so both the upper and lower parts get covered instead of only one. More thorough than holding a single position.

  1. Place the ball of one foot against the wall with the heel on the floor
  2. Straighten that leg and lean in until you feel the upper calf stretch
  3. Hold there, then slide the foot down so the angle becomes shallower
  4. Bend the knee slightly to move the stretch lower into the calf
  5. Hold each position for twenty seconds, then swap legs
ea_calve_stretch_from_wall_to_floor

Calves Stretch on Step

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeLetting the heel drop below a step uses gravity and your own bodyweight for the stretch, which reaches further than pushing against a wall. The easiest calf stretch to fit into a normal day.

  1. Stand on a step with the balls of both feet on the edge, heels hanging off
  2. Hold a rail or wall for balance
  3. Let both heels sink slowly below the level of the step
  4. Keep the legs straight to reach the upper calf, or bend the knees for the lower part
  5. Hold for thirty seconds, then rise back up under control
ea_calves_stretch_on_step knee

Child Pose Lower Back Stretch

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeLengthens the lower back and the hips in a position that takes all the load off the spine, which is why it is the standard place to rest between harder movements or after a heavy session.

  1. Kneel on the floor with your big toes together and knees apart
  2. Sit your hips back toward your heels
  3. Walk your hands forward and lower your chest between your thighs
  4. Rest your forehead on the mat and let your shoulders relax
  5. Breathe into your lower back and hold for thirty seconds or longer
ea_child_pose_lower_back_stretch

Cobra Stretch

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeExtends the spine backwards, the opposite of the forward-folded position most people hold all day. It also stretches the front of the stomach and hips, which shorten from sitting.

  1. Lie face down with your palms under your shoulders and elbows tucked in
  2. Press the tops of your feet and your hips into the floor
  3. Push through your hands to lift your chest, keeping your hips down
  4. Go only as far as feels comfortable in the lower back — the elbows may stay bent
  5. Hold for twenty seconds, breathing steadily, then lower down slowly
ea_cobra_stretch lower_backupper_back

Crescent Moon Pose Quad Stretch

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeStretches the front of the hip and thigh of the back leg at once, which is the pair that tightens from sitting and limits how far the hip can extend when you walk or run.

  1. Kneel on one knee with the other foot forward, both bent to about ninety degrees
  2. Squeeze the glute of the kneeling leg to push that hip forward
  3. Raise both arms overhead and lengthen through your side
  4. Keep your ribs down so the stretch stays in the hip, not the lower back
  5. Hold for thirty seconds, then change sides
ea_crescent_moon_pose_quad_stretch

Crescent Moon Pose Quad Stretch with Block

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeThe same hip and thigh stretch with a block under the hands, so you can hold the position without needing the balance the full version demands. The version to use while the hip is still tight.

  1. Kneel on one knee with the other foot forward and a block beside the front foot
  2. Rest one or both hands on the block to steady yourself
  3. Push the hip of the kneeling leg forward by squeezing that glute
  4. Keep your torso upright and your ribs pulled down
  5. Hold for thirty seconds, then swap legs
ea_crescent_moon_pose_quad_stretch_with_block

Cross Body Elbow Pull Shoulder Stretch

Stretching - Mobility

PurposePulling by the elbow rather than the wrist keeps the pressure off the shoulder joint and puts the stretch where it belongs — across the back of the shoulder, which tightens after pressing and throwing.

  1. Stand tall and bring one arm straight across your chest
  2. Hook the opposite hand behind that elbow, not the forearm
  3. Draw the arm gently across your body until you feel the back of the shoulder stretch
  4. Keep both shoulders down and facing forward — do not rotate the torso
  5. Hold for twenty to thirty seconds, then change arms
ea_cross_body_elbow_pull_shoulder_stretch

Cross Body Shoulder Stretch

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeThe simplest way to open the back of the shoulder, which is the area that closes up after a session of rows and pull-ups. Quick enough to do between sets.

  1. Stand or sit tall with your shoulders level
  2. Reach one arm straight across the front of your chest
  3. Support it with the other forearm and draw it closer to your body
  4. Keep the working shoulder pressed down, away from your ear
  5. Hold for twenty seconds, then do the other side
ea_cross_body_shoulder_stretch

Foam Roller Back

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeRolling the upper back restores the extension that sitting takes away, which is what lets you hold a bar overhead or keep the chest up in a squat. Stay above the ribs — never roll the lower back.

  1. Lie on your back with a foam roller across your upper back, below the shoulder blades
  2. Support your head with your hands and lift your hips off the floor
  3. Roll slowly up and down between the shoulder blades and the base of the neck
  4. Pause on any tight spot and breathe for a few seconds
  5. Stop at the bottom of the ribs — do not roll onto the lower back
ea_foam_roller_back upper_back

Foam Roller Calves

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeTight calves limit how far the ankle bends, which shows up as heels lifting in a squat and as a shortened stride when running. Rolling them is faster than stretching at restoring that movement.

  1. Sit on the floor with a foam roller under one calf and the other leg crossed over it
  2. Press your hands into the floor to lift your hips
  3. Roll slowly from just above the ankle to just below the knee
  4. Stop on tight spots and rotate the leg in and out to reach the sides
  5. Spend about a minute per leg, then switch
ea_foam_roller_calves

Foam Roller Lateral Quads

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeThe outside of the thigh gets tight in anyone who runs or cycles, and that tightness pulls on the outside of the knee. This is usually the most uncomfortable rolling there is, and often the most useful.

  1. Lie on your side with a foam roller under the outside of one thigh
  2. Support yourself on your forearm and the opposite foot
  3. Roll slowly from just below the hip to just above the knee
  4. Never roll directly over the knee or the hip bone
  5. Pause on the tightest spots and breathe, then change sides
ea_foam_roller_lateral_quads

Foam Roller Quads-

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeRolling the front of the thigh before training helps the knee bend more freely, and after training it helps with the stiffness that follows heavy squatting. One of the few rolling spots that is easy to reach.

  1. Lie face down with a foam roller under the front of both thighs
  2. Support yourself on your forearms with your elbows under your shoulders
  3. Roll slowly from just below the hips to just above the knees
  4. Pause on tender areas and breathe until they ease
  5. Roll one leg at a time if you want more pressure
ea_foam_roller_quads

Forearms Pull with Opposite Hand Stretch

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeStretches the forearm muscles that grip all day, whether on a bar or a keyboard. Doing it regularly is one of the few things that genuinely helps with elbow pain from overuse.

  1. Extend one arm straight out in front of you at shoulder height, palm down
  2. Use the opposite hand to pull the fingers gently back toward you
  3. Keep the extended elbow straight throughout
  4. Hold, then turn the palm up and pull the fingers down for the other side of the forearm
  5. Hold each position for twenty seconds, then change arms
ea_forearms_pull_with_opposite_hand_stretch

Forearms Stretch on Wall

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeUses the wall so you can stretch both forearms at once and control the intensity with your own bodyweight. Better than the hand-pull version when the forearms are properly tight.

  1. Stand facing a wall and place both palms flat on it at chest height, fingers up
  2. Keep your arms straight and your shoulders down
  3. Step back slightly and press your palms into the wall
  4. Lean away until you feel the stretch along the underside of both forearms
  5. Hold for thirty seconds, breathing steadily
ea_forearms_stretch_on_wall

Forearms Stretch on Wall Fingers Facing Down

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeTurning the fingers down reaches the muscles on the top of the forearm — the side connected to the outer elbow, which is where the ache from too much gripping usually settles.

  1. Face a wall and place both palms on it with the fingers pointing straight down
  2. Keep your arms straight and your elbows soft, not locked hard
  3. Press the palms flat against the wall
  4. Lean in gently until you feel the stretch across the top of the forearms
  5. Hold for twenty to thirty seconds without forcing it
ea_forearms_stretch_on_wall_fingers_facing_down

Half Neck Rolls

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeReleases the neck without taking it backwards, which is the direction that causes trouble. Half rolls are the safe version and still reach the muscles that stiffen from screens and from carrying stress.

  1. Sit or stand tall with your shoulders relaxed and down
  2. Drop your chin toward your chest
  3. Roll your head slowly to one side until your ear moves toward that shoulder
  4. Roll back through the middle to the other side, keeping the chin low the whole time
  5. Never roll the head backwards; continue for the set time
ea_half_neck_rolls neck

Hands Clapped Forearms Stretch

Stretching - Mobility

PurposePressing the palms together and lowering them stretches both forearms and wrists evenly, which matters for anyone doing push-ups, front squats or handstands — all of which need the wrist to bend back.

  1. Stand or sit tall and press your palms together in front of your chest
  2. Keep the palms touching along their whole length
  3. Lower the hands slowly toward your stomach, keeping the elbows out
  4. Stop when you feel the stretch across the wrists and forearms
  5. Hold for twenty to thirty seconds, breathing normally
ea_hands_clapped_forearms_stretch

Lats Stretch Elbow on Wall

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeThe lats run from the arm to the lower back, so when they are tight they limit how far the arms go overhead. This stretch is often what makes an overhead press stop pinching.

  1. Stand a step away from a wall and place one elbow on it at about head height
  2. Step back and hinge at the hips so your chest drops toward the floor
  3. Let your head sink between your arms and lengthen through the side
  4. Breathe into the side of your ribs, where the stretch should be felt
  5. Hold for thirty seconds, then change sides
ea_lats_stretch_elbow_on_wall

Lats Stretch on Wall

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeReaching both hands to a wall and sitting the hips back stretches both lats at once. Quick, needs nothing, and it is the standard thing to do before any overhead lifting.

  1. Stand facing a wall and place both hands on it at about head height
  2. Walk your feet back until your arms are straight
  3. Push your hips back and let your chest sink toward the floor
  4. Keep your arms straight and your head between your upper arms
  5. Hold for thirty seconds, breathing into the sides of your back
ea_lats_stretch_on_wall

Lying Bent Knee Cross Glutes Stretch

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeReaches the deep muscles at the back of the hip, which tighten from sitting and can press on the nerve that runs down the leg. One of the more effective positions for hip and lower back tightness.

  1. Lie on your back with both knees bent and feet flat
  2. Cross one ankle over the opposite knee to make a figure four
  3. Reach through the gap and hold the back of the supporting thigh
  4. Draw that leg toward your chest until you feel the stretch in the crossed hip
  5. Hold for thirty seconds, keeping your head and shoulders on the floor, then swap
ea_lying_bent_knee_cross_glutes_stretch

Lying Face Down Quadriceps Stretch

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeStretches the front of the thigh with the hip flat on the floor, which stops you cheating by arching your back. That makes it a truer stretch than the standing version most people do.

  1. Lie face down with your forehead resting on your free arm
  2. Bend one knee and reach back to hold that ankle or foot
  3. Draw the heel toward your backside, keeping the hip pressed into the floor
  4. Stop as soon as you feel the front of the thigh stretch, not the knee
  5. Hold for thirty seconds, then change legs
ea_lying_face_down_quadriceps_stretch

Lying Knee Hugs Lower Back Stretch

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeRounds the lower back gently in the safest possible position, which relieves the compression that builds up from standing, lifting and sitting. Usually the first thing that helps a stiff back in the morning.

  1. Lie on your back with your legs straight
  2. Draw both knees toward your chest and wrap your arms around them
  3. Pull them in gently until your lower back rounds against the floor
  4. Keep your head and shoulders relaxed on the ground
  5. Hold for thirty seconds, breathing into the lower back
ea_lying_knee_hugs_lower_back_stretch

Lying Knee Pull Glutes Stretch

Stretching - Mobility

PurposePulling one knee across the body reaches the outside of the hip, which is where tightness builds in runners and in anyone who sits with their legs crossed. Gentler than the figure-four version.

  1. Lie on your back with your legs straight and arms out to the sides
  2. Bend one knee and draw it up toward your chest
  3. Use the opposite hand to guide that knee across your body toward the floor
  4. Keep both shoulders flat on the ground as the knee crosses over
  5. Hold for thirty seconds, then bring it back and change legs
ea_lying_knee_pull_glutes_stretch

Lying Knees to Floor Lower Back Stretch

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeA gentle rotation of the spine that opens the lower back and the front of the chest at the same time. One of the safest ways to restore rotation, which the back loses faster than any other movement.

  1. Lie on your back with your knees bent and your arms out wide
  2. Keep your knees together and your feet on the floor
  3. Let both knees fall slowly to one side toward the ground
  4. Turn your head the opposite way and keep both shoulders on the floor
  5. Hold for thirty seconds, then bring the knees through the middle to the other side
ea_lying_knees_to_floor_lower_back_stretch

Lying Single Leg Extended on Wall Hamstrings Stretch

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeThe wall holds the leg for you, so the hamstring can relax into the stretch instead of working to hold the position. That makes it far more effective than reaching for your toes while standing.

  1. Lie on your back beside a doorway or a wall corner
  2. Raise one leg and rest it flat against the wall, keeping it as straight as you can
  3. Let the other leg lie flat along the floor
  4. Slide your hips closer to the wall to increase the stretch
  5. Hold for thirty to sixty seconds, then change legs
ea_lying_single_leg_extended_on_wall_hamstrings_stretch

Revolved Head to Knee

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeCombines a hamstring stretch with a side bend, so the back of the leg and the whole side of the torso lengthen together. It reaches the space between the ribs, which almost nothing else does.

  1. Sit with one leg straight out to the side and the other foot tucked toward your groin
  2. Rest the same-side forearm on the straight leg
  3. Reach the opposite arm overhead and over toward that foot
  4. Turn your chest slightly upward rather than folding forward
  5. Hold for thirty seconds, breathing into the top ribs, then switch sides
ea_revolved_head_to_knee

Seated Figure Four with Twist Glute Stretch

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeAdding a twist to the figure four reaches deeper into the back of the hip and stretches the lower back at the same time. Can be done in a chair, which makes it practical during a working day.

  1. Sit tall on the floor or a chair and cross one ankle over the opposite knee
  2. Let the crossed knee fall open to the side
  3. Place the opposite hand on that knee and the other hand behind you
  4. Turn your chest toward the crossed leg, lengthening as you go
  5. Hold for thirty seconds, then unwind slowly and change sides
ea_seated_figure_four_with_twist_glute_stretch hipwrist

Seated Single Leg Toe Touch Hamstring Stretch

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeOne leg at a time lets you work on the tighter side without the looser one hiding it. Hamstring tightness is almost always uneven, and a two-leg stretch never shows you that.

  1. Sit on the floor with one leg straight out and the other bent, foot to the inner thigh
  2. Sit up tall and turn your chest toward the straight leg
  3. Hinge forward from the hips, not by rounding your back
  4. Reach toward the foot of the straight leg until you feel the stretch behind the thigh
  5. Hold for thirty seconds, then change legs
ea_seated_single_leg_toe_touch_hamstring_stretch lower_back

Seated Toe Touch Hamstrings Stretch

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeThe most familiar hamstring stretch there is. Done from the hips with a flat back it lengthens the hamstrings; done by rounding the back it mostly stretches the spine instead, which is not the point.

  1. Sit on the floor with both legs straight out in front of you
  2. Sit up tall and lengthen through the top of your head
  3. Hinge forward from the hips, keeping your back as flat as you can
  4. Reach toward your feet and stop where the stretch is felt behind the thighs
  5. Hold for thirty seconds, breathing out as you settle deeper
ea_seated_toe_touch_hamstrings_stretch lower_back

Side Bend Standing Lats Stretch

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeOpens the whole side of the body from the hip to the hand, including the lats and the muscles between the ribs. Takes ten seconds and needs no equipment, which makes it easy to do often.

  1. Stand tall with your feet hip width apart
  2. Reach one arm straight overhead and hold the wrist with the other hand
  3. Lengthen upward first, then bend to the opposite side
  4. Keep both feet flat and your hips facing forward
  5. Hold for twenty seconds, then come back up and do the other side
ea_side_bend_standing_lats_stretch

Side Chest Stretch on Wall

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeOpens one side of the chest at a time, which lets you spend longer on the tighter side. Chest tightness is often asymmetric, especially in people who work at a desk with a mouse.

  1. Stand beside a wall and place one palm flat on it behind you at shoulder height
  2. Keep that arm straight and the shoulder pressed down
  3. Turn your body slowly away from the wall
  4. Stop when you feel the stretch across the front of the chest and shoulder
  5. Hold for twenty to thirty seconds, then change sides
ea_side_chest_stretch_on_wall

Single Arm Extended Pull Downwards Biceps Stretch

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeStretches the biceps and the front of the shoulder without needing a wall, so it can be done anywhere. Useful right after a session of curls or pulling, when that area is still shortened.

  1. Stand tall and extend one arm straight down and slightly behind you
  2. Turn the palm to face backwards and away from your body
  3. Use the other hand to press gently down on that hand
  4. Keep the elbow locked straight and the shoulder pulled down
  5. Hold for twenty seconds, then change arms
ea_single_arm_extended_pull_downwards_biceps_stretch

Single Arm Palm Down on Wall Biceps Stretch

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeTurning the palm down changes which part of the biceps and forearm gets stretched, reaching fibres the thumb-down version misses. Worth doing both if the arm feels tight after heavy pulling.

  1. Stand side-on to a wall and place one palm flat on it behind you, fingers pointing back
  2. Keep the arm straight and at about shoulder height
  3. Press the palm into the wall and keep the shoulder down
  4. Rotate your torso away from the wall until you feel the stretch
  5. Hold for twenty seconds, then change arms
ea_single_arm_palm_down_on_wall_biceps_stretch

Single Arm on Wall Side Biceps Stretch

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeThe wall lets you control the intensity precisely by turning your body, which makes it the best biceps stretch for an arm that is genuinely tight. Also opens the front of that shoulder.

  1. Stand side-on to a wall and place one palm on it behind you at shoulder height
  2. Straighten that arm fully with the thumb pointing down
  3. Keep the shoulder pressed down away from your ear
  4. Turn your chest slowly away from the wall until the biceps stretches
  5. Hold for twenty to thirty seconds, then swap sides
ea_single_arm_on_wall_side_biceps_stretch

Standing Straight-leg Hamstring Stretch

Stretching - Mobility

PurposeA hamstring stretch that needs nothing at all and can be done anywhere, including between sets. Hinge from the hips rather than rounding the back — otherwise the stretch lands on the spine instead.

  1. Stand tall and step one foot forward with the heel on the floor and toes up
  2. Keep the front leg straight and soften the back knee
  3. Push your hips back and hinge forward with a flat back
  4. Rest your hands on the bent thigh for support
  5. Hold for twenty to thirty seconds, then change legs
ea_standing_straight_leg_hamstring_stretch

Band Lying Press Down

Triceps

PurposeLying down pins your shoulder blades to the floor, so the shoulders cannot join in and the triceps has to straighten the arm on its own. The band pulls hardest at full extension, which is exactly where the triceps is strongest.

  1. Anchor the band to something solid behind your head and lie on your back
  2. Hold an end in each hand and bring your elbows up so the upper arms point at the ceiling
  3. Keep the upper arms still — only the forearms will move
  4. Straighten your elbows so your hands travel toward your hips and the band stretches
  5. Bend the elbows slowly to bring your hands back beside your ears
ea_band_lying_press_down shoulder

Band Skullcrusher

Triceps

PurposeLoads the triceps with the arms overhead, which stretches the long head — the part that runs to the shoulder blade and is missed by every pushdown. A band does this without the elbow pressure a bar puts on the joint in the same position.

  1. Anchor the band low behind you and lie on a bench or the floor with your head toward the anchor
  2. Hold both ends and press your arms straight up so the hands are over your shoulders
  3. Keep the upper arms vertical and locked in place
  4. Bend only the elbows to lower your hands toward your forehead
  5. Straighten the arms back to the start, stopping just short of locking the elbows
ea_band_skullcrusher

Band Triceps Pushdown Single Arm

Triceps

PurposeOne arm at a time, so a stronger triceps cannot cover for a weaker one — which matters because a lagging triceps is usually what stalls a bench press. A band makes this possible anywhere, without a cable stack.

  1. Anchor the band above head height and stand facing it, one step back
  2. Take the end in one hand with the elbow bent and tucked against your ribs
  3. Put the other hand on that elbow so you can feel it stay in place
  4. Push the hand down until the arm is straight, keeping the elbow pinned
  5. Let the band pull the hand back up slowly, then repeat and change arms
ea_band_triceps_pushdown_single_arm elbow

Cable Cross Pushdown

Triceps

PurposeCrossing the cables in front of you pulls each arm outward as well as up, so the triceps has to hold the arm in line as it straightens. That extra job hits the outer head, the one that gives the arm its shape just above the elbow.

  1. Set both pulleys at head height and take the left handle in your right hand and the right in your left
  2. Stand in the middle so the cables cross in front of your chest, elbows bent and at your sides
  3. Brace your stomach and lean forward very slightly from the hips
  4. Push both hands down and slightly outward until the arms are straight
  5. Return slowly to the bent position without letting the elbows drift forward
ea_cable_cross_pushdown elbow

Dumbbell Skullcrusher

Triceps

PurposeThe classic mass builder for the triceps: arms overhead puts the long head on stretch, and separate dumbbells let each wrist find an angle the elbow is comfortable with, which a straight bar does not allow.

  1. Lie on a bench with a dumbbell in each hand and press them up over your shoulders, palms facing each other
  2. Keep your upper arms vertical for the whole set
  3. Bend the elbows to lower the dumbbells down beside your ears
  4. Stop when your forearms pass just below parallel with the floor
  5. Straighten the arms back to the top without letting the elbows flare outward
ea_dumbbell_skullcrusher

Floor Tricep Dip

Triceps

PurposeThe triceps exercise that needs nothing at all — no bench, no weights, no band. Your feet stay on the floor, so you can make it as light or as hard as you need by walking them in or out, which makes it a safe first dip.

  1. Sit on the floor with your knees bent and feet flat, hands on the floor behind your hips, fingers pointing at your feet
  2. Press through your hands to lift your hips off the floor
  3. Keep your chest open and your shoulders pulled down away from your ears
  4. Bend the elbows straight back to lower your hips toward the floor
  5. Push back up until the arms are straight, without letting your hips touch down
ea_floor_tricep_dip elbowshoulderwrist

Kettlebell Decline Skull Crusher

Triceps

PurposeThe decline angle keeps tension on the triceps at the top, where a flat bench lets the arms rest under the weight. The bell hanging below your hand also pulls the elbow further back, adding stretch at the bottom.

  1. Set a bench to a slight decline and lie down with your feet hooked under the pads
  2. Hold a kettlebell in each hand and press them up so your arms point straight at the ceiling
  3. Keep the upper arms fixed and vertical
  4. Bend the elbows to lower the bells toward the top of your head
  5. Straighten the arms back up, stopping just before the elbows lock
ea_kettlebell_decline_skull_crusher elbow

Kettlebell Skull Crusher

Triceps

PurposeSame stretch as the dumbbell version, but the bell hangs behind the hand, so the load sits further from the elbow and the triceps has to control a longer lever. Less weight does more work here.

  1. Lie on a bench with a kettlebell in each hand, bells resting against the back of your forearms
  2. Press the arms straight up over your shoulders
  3. Hold the upper arms still and vertical
  4. Bend the elbows and let the bells travel down past your ears
  5. Extend the arms back to the start under control
ea_kettlebell_skull_crusher elbow

Kettlebell Standing Tricep Extension

Triceps

PurposeStanding means your stomach and lower back have to hold you upright while a weight sits behind your head — so this trains the triceps and the brace to keep the ribs down at the same time.

  1. Stand with feet hip width apart and hold one kettlebell by the horns with both hands
  2. Press it overhead until your arms are straight, then let the bell rest behind your head
  3. Squeeze your stomach so your ribs do not flare forward
  4. Bend the elbows to lower the bell behind your head, keeping the upper arms beside your ears
  5. Straighten the arms back overhead without arching your lower back
ea_kettlebell_standing_tricep_extension elbow

Landmine Lying Tricep Extension

Triceps

PurposeThe landmine's arc keeps the bar travelling away from your face instead of toward it, which removes the one thing that makes people nervous about lying extensions. Both hands on one bar also let you load heavier than a pair of dumbbells.

  1. Set a bench in front of a landmine so the loaded end reaches over your head when you lie down
  2. Lie back and take the end of the bar with both hands, arms pressed straight up
  3. Keep your upper arms vertical and your shoulder blades flat on the bench
  4. Bend the elbows to let the bar swing down behind your head along its arc
  5. Push the bar back up to straight arms following the same arc
ea_landmine_lying_tricep_extension elbow

Plate Curl to Overhead Press to Tricep Extension

Triceps

PurposeThree movements chained without putting the plate down: biceps, then shoulders, then triceps. Because the weight never rests, your heart rate climbs — this is arm work that doubles as conditioning when time is short.

  1. Hold a plate at the sides with both hands, arms hanging in front of your hips
  2. Curl it up to your chest with the elbows close to your body
  3. Press it straight overhead until your arms lock out
  4. Bend the elbows to lower the plate behind your head, then push it back overhead
  5. Lower it to your chest and back down to your hips — that is one full repetition
ea_plate_curl_to_overhead_press_to_tricep_extension elbowshoulder

Plate Overhead Tricep Extension

Triceps

PurposeGets the long head of the triceps on full stretch with the simplest equipment there is. Gripping a plate by the edges also makes your fingers work, so grip gets trained alongside the arm.

  1. Stand tall and hold a weight plate at the sides with both hands
  2. Press it overhead until your arms are straight
  3. Keep your elbows pointing forward and close together, not flaring out
  4. Bend the elbows to lower the plate down behind your head as far as is comfortable
  5. Push it back overhead to straight arms, keeping your ribs down and back flat
ea_plate_overhead_tricep_extension elbowshoulder

Tricep Rope Extension on Crossover Machine

Triceps

PurposeThe rope lets your hands separate at the bottom, so the arms finish fully straight and turned slightly outward — the position where the triceps contracts hardest. A straight bar locks the hands together and stops short of it.

  1. Attach a rope to the high pulley and stand facing the machine, one step back
  2. Take one end in each hand with the thumbs on top and pull your elbows to your sides
  3. Lean forward very slightly and brace your stomach
  4. Push the rope down and pull the ends apart as your arms straighten
  5. Return slowly, letting the rope come back together until the forearms are parallel to the floor
ea_tricep_rope_extension_on_crossover_machine elbow

Bow Pose

Yoga

PurposeOpens the entire front of the body at once — hips, stomach, chest and shoulders — which is the whole surface that shortens from sitting. One of the strongest counters to a desk-bound day.

  1. Lie face down with your arms by your sides and forehead on the mat
  2. Bend both knees and reach back to hold your ankles from the outside
  3. Press your feet back into your hands rather than pulling with your arms
  4. Let that pressure lift your chest and thighs off the floor
  5. Breathe steadily and hold for fifteen to thirty seconds, then release slowly
ea_bow_pose upper_back

Cat Pose

Yoga

PurposeRounding the spine on all fours restores movement between the vertebrae that a day of sitting still takes away. Paired with its opposite, it is the standard way to warm the back up before anything else.

  1. Start on hands and knees with wrists under shoulders and knees under hips
  2. Keep the spine long and neutral to begin
  3. Breathe out and round your back toward the ceiling, one segment at a time
  4. Let your head drop and draw your stomach up toward your spine
  5. Hold for a breath, then return to neutral or move into the opposite arch
ea_cat_pose

Chair Pose

Yoga

PurposeHolds a squat position with the arms overhead, which works the legs and asks the shoulders and upper back to stay open under load. Simple, and it burns much sooner than it looks like it should.

  1. Stand with your feet together or hip width apart
  2. Bend your knees and sit your hips back as if lowering into a chair
  3. Keep your weight in your heels and your chest lifted
  4. Raise both arms overhead alongside your ears, palms facing each other
  5. Hold for thirty seconds, breathing steadily, then stand up slowly
ea_chair_pose

Child Pose Arms Extended Left Right

Yoga

PurposeWalking the hands to one side turns the rest position into a side stretch, reaching the lats and the space between the ribs. A way to get two things from one shape while you catch your breath.

  1. Kneel with your big toes together and your knees wide apart
  2. Sit your hips back toward your heels and lower your chest to the floor
  3. Walk both hands across to one side, keeping the hips centred
  4. Feel the stretch down the opposite side of your ribs and back
  5. Hold for thirty seconds, then walk the hands across to the other side
ea_child_pose_arms_extended_left_right

Child Pose Arms on Side

Yoga

PurposeThe most restful version, with the arms back and the shoulders completely released. Used to slow the breathing down between hard efforts, or at the end of a session to finish calm.

  1. Kneel and sit your hips back onto your heels
  2. Bring your knees together or slightly apart, whichever is comfortable
  3. Fold forward and rest your forehead on the mat
  4. Lay your arms back alongside your body with the palms facing up
  5. Let the shoulders drop and breathe slowly for thirty seconds or more
ea_child_pose_arms_on_side

Child Pose Elbows on Block

Yoga

PurposeRaising the elbows on a block deepens the shoulder stretch, which turns a rest pose into targeted work for overhead range. Useful for anyone whose arms will not go straight up beside the ears.

  1. Kneel with your knees wide and sit your hips back toward your heels
  2. Place a block in front of you and rest both elbows on it
  3. Bring your palms together behind your head
  4. Let your chest sink toward the floor between your arms
  5. Hold for thirty seconds, breathing into the shoulders and upper back
ea_child_pose_elbows_on_block

Crescent Moon Pose

Yoga

PurposeA lunge with the arms overhead that stretches the front of the back hip while the front leg works to hold you up. It opens the hip and challenges balance in the same shape.

  1. Step one foot well forward into a lunge with the back heel lifted
  2. Bend the front knee to about ninety degrees over the ankle
  3. Squeeze the back glute to push that hip forward
  4. Raise both arms overhead and lengthen upward through your fingers
  5. Hold for thirty seconds, breathing steadily, then change legs
ea_crescent_moon_pose

Criss Cross Bow Tie Pose

Yoga

PurposeCrossing the arms behind the back opens both shoulders in a direction almost nothing else reaches. It targets exactly the tightness that comes from spending the day with the arms in front of you.

  1. Lie face down or kneel tall with your shoulders relaxed
  2. Reach both arms behind your back and cross them at the forearms
  3. Take hold of the opposite upper arm or elbow if you can reach
  4. Draw the shoulder blades together and let the chest open
  5. Hold for twenty to thirty seconds, then switch which arm is on top
ea_criss_cross_bow_tie_pose

Crow Pose

Yoga
